111744.e: The walls of the small blood vessels become leakier. Fluid and defence cells get into the tissue, which makes it swell.
111744.m: Leaking fluid makes inflamed tissue swell.

111745.q: Which ending do many medical names for inflammations have?
111745.e: Examples are bronchitis and arthritis. The ending “-oma”, on the other hand, often stands for a growth, and “-algia” for pain.

111746.e: The ending “-itis” stands for inflammation. In bronchitis, the branches of the windpipe are inflamed.
111746.m: Bronchitis is an inflammation of the bronchi.

111747.q: Which cells move into the tissue during inflammation to fight germs?
111747.e: White blood cells are part of the body's defences. During inflammation they move out of the blood vessels into the tissue and fight germs.
111747.m: White blood cells fight germs during inflammation.

111748.q: Why does an inflamed spot often hurt?
a: Messenger substances and the swelling irritate the pain nerves
111748.e: During inflammation, messenger substances are released and the tissue swells. Both irritate the nerves, which is why the spot hurts.

111749.q: What is pus mainly made of?
a: Dead defence cells, germs and bits of tissue
Fat and oil from the skin
111749.e: Pus forms when many defence cells die while fighting bacteria. Together with germs and broken-down tissue they form a thick fluid.
111749.m: Pus is mainly made of dead defence cells.

111750.q: What is an enclosed collection of pus in a newly formed cavity in the tissue called?
111750.e: In an abscess, tissue is broken down and a cavity full of pus forms. A haematoma, on the other hand, is a bruise.
111750.m: An abscess is a cavity of pus in the tissue.

111751.q: What is a pus-filled inflammation of a hair follicle and the area around it called?
111751.e: A boil usually develops from bacteria that get into a hair follicle. A painful, pus-filled lump forms.
111751.m: A boil is an inflamed, pus-filled hair follicle.

111752.e: Pus is usually yellowish to greenish and cloudy. The colour comes from the many cells and their parts.
111752.m: Pus is usually yellowish and cloudy.

111753.q: Which bacteria are among the most common causes of pus?
111753.e: Staphylococcus aureus is one of the main causes of pus-filled skin and wound infections. Lactic acid bacteria, on the other hand, are used for yoghurt, for example.

111754.q: Why should you not squeeze a pus-filled spot with dirty fingers?
111754.e: When you squeeze, bacteria can get deeper into the tissue. Then the inflammation can get bigger.
111754.m: It is better not to squeeze pus-filled spots.

111755.q: Which cells fight bacteria during inflammation and form pus in the process?
111755.e: White blood cells move to the inflammation and eat bacteria. Many die in the process and form pus together with the germs.
111755.m: Pus forms from dead white blood cells.

111756.q: What is a small blister on the skin filled with pus called?
111756.e: A pustule is a pus blister, as found in acne, for example. A papule is a small bump without pus.
111756.m: A pustule is a pus blister.

111757.q: What job do the memory cells of the immune system do?
a: Recognise a germ again and fight it quickly
111757.e: Memory cells stay in the body after an infection. If they meet the same germ again, they immediately start a strong defence.
111757.m: Memory cells remember germs that were fought before.

111758.q: Which blood cells do memory cells belong to?
111758.e: White blood cells are the body's defence cells. Memory cells are a special kind of them.
111758.m: Memory cells are white blood cells.

111759.q: Why do you usually get chickenpox only once in your life?
a: Memory cells recognise the virus the next time
The virus only occurs in children
The skin becomes impenetrable with age
The virus dies out in summer
111759.e: After the first illness, long-lasting immunity remains. Memory cells make sure that a new infection is usually fought off without any signs of illness.
111759.m: Anyone who has had chickenpox is usually protected for life.

111760.q: How does a vaccination make use of memory cells?
a: The body makes them without really getting ill
It kills all the old memory cells
It turns memory cells into red blood cells
It prevents memory cells from forming
111760.e: A vaccine contains weakened or killed germs or parts of them. The immune system reacts to them and creates memory cells.
111760.m: A vaccination trains the immune memory.

111761.q: Where in the body are the white blood cells made from which memory cells develop?
111761.e: All blood cells, including white blood cells, are made in the red bone marrow. Some of them later become memory cells.
111761.m: Defence cells are made in the bone marrow.

111762.q: How long can some memory cells survive in the body?
111762.e: Many memory cells are very long-lived. That is why getting over an illness or having a vaccination often protects you for a very long time.
111762.m: Memory cells can live for decades.

111763.q: How does the immune system react the second time it meets the same germ?
a: Exactly the same as the first time
111763.e: The first time, the defences need a few days. The second time, the memory cells recognise the germ immediately and the defence starts faster and more strongly.
111763.m: The second time, the body defends itself faster.

111764.q: What does a booster vaccination do?
a: It raises the number of memory cells and antibodies again
It replaces the making of red blood cells
111764.e: With some vaccinations, the protection fades over time. Another dose refreshes the immune memory.
111764.m: A booster vaccination strengthens the immune memory.

111765.q: What kind of organ is the thymus?
111765.e: Defence cells are trained in the thymus. So it serves the body's defence, not digestion, the senses or excretion.
111765.m: The thymus is an organ of the immune system.

111766.q: Which defence cells mature in the thymus?
111766.e: In the thymus these cells are trained and mature into working defence cells. They are also named after this organ.
111766.m: T cells mature in the thymus.

111767.q: What would happen if a child were born without a working thymus?
111767.e: Without a thymus, no mature T cells can form. The body then lacks an important part of its defences, and infections become very dangerous.
111767.m: Without a thymus, the body lacks an important part of its defences.

111768.q: How does the thymus change over the course of life?
a: It shrinks and partly turns into fatty tissue
It keeps growing into old age
It turns to bone and becomes a rib
It moves from the chest into the abdomen
111768.e: The thymus is large and active in children. In adults it gets smaller and smaller and is mostly replaced by fat.

111769.q: Where do the immature precursor cells come from that mature in the thymus?
111769.e: All blood cells are made in the bone marrow. Some of the precursors of the lymphocytes travel from there through the blood to the thymus.
111769.m: The precursors of the thymus cells come from the bone marrow.

111770.q: What do T cells learn in the thymus?
a: To tell the body's own cells from foreign ones
111770.e: In the thymus, T cells that would attack the body itself are sorted out. The cells that remain only fight foreign substances.
111770.m: In the thymus, T cells learn to spare the body itself.

111771.q: In cooking, what is the thymus of a calf known as?
111771.e: Veal sweetbreads, called Kalbsmilken in Switzerland, are the thymus of young calves. Tripe, on the other hand, is part of a cow's stomach.
111771.m: Veal sweetbreads are the thymus of a calf.

111772.q: How many lobes does the thymus have?
111772.e: The thymus has a left and a right lobe. These are divided into many small lobules.

111773.q: What is typical of the non-specific defence?
a: It works immediately against many different germs
It is only aimed at a single germ
It only starts after several weeks
It only comes from a vaccination
111773.e: The non-specific defence does not tell individual germs apart precisely. Instead it reacts very quickly, within the first minutes to hours.
111773.m: The non-specific defence reacts immediately, but not in a targeted way.

111774.q: What is the non-specific defence also called?
111774.e: You are born with the non-specific defence. The specific defence, on the other hand, is only acquired during life.

111775.q: Which substance in the stomach kills many swallowed germs?
111775.e: Stomach juice contains hydrochloric acid and is very acidic. Many bacteria do not survive this acidic environment.

111776.q: How do tears protect the eye from bacteria?
a: They wash germs away and contain a substance that attacks bacteria
They cool the eye down a lot
They colour the bacteria so they can be seen
111776.e: Tears rinse dirt and germs out of the eye. They also contain an enzyme that destroys the walls of bacteria.
111776.m: Tears are part of the body's own defences.

111777.q: How does healthy skin protect against germs?
a: It forms a tight barrier to the outside
It makes antibodies against every virus
It lets T cells mature in it
It filters the lymph from the tissue
111777.e: The outer horny layer of the skin cannot be penetrated by most germs. Only through injuries can they get in easily.
111777.m: Unbroken skin keeps most germs out.

111778.q: How can fever help the body's defences?
a: It slows down some germs and speeds up defence processes
It replaces the making of antibodies
It stops you ever getting ill again
111778.e: Many germs multiply less well at a raised temperature. At the same time, some defence reactions run faster.
111778.m: Fever helps the body's own defences.

111779.q: Which cells of the innate defence kill body cells infected by viruses?
111779.e: Natural killer cells recognise sick body cells by changed features on their surface. They do not need any previous training for this.
111779.m: Natural killer cells kill infected cells immediately.

111780.q: How do harmless bacteria on the skin and in the gut protect against germs?
a: They take up the space and food the germs need
They make antibodies against the germs
They let T cells mature in the gut
111780.e: The natural bacterial flora covers the skin and gut thickly. This leaves harmful germs hardly any space or food to settle.
111780.m: Useful bacteria crowd out harmful germs.

111781.q: What is typical of the specific defence?
a: It is aimed specifically at one particular germ
It works the same against all germs
It consists only of the skin
It only works in the stomach
111781.e: The specific defence recognises exact features of a germ. For this it needs more time the first time it meets it.
111781.m: The specific defence fights germs in a targeted way.

111782.q: What does the specific defence make that is aimed at one particular germ?
111782.e: Certain white blood cells make antibodies that fit exactly one germ. Stomach acid, skin oil and tears, on the other hand, work the same against all germs.
111782.m: Antibodies fight germs in a targeted way.

111783.q: What is a foreign substance called against which the body makes antibodies?
111783.e: An antigen is a feature, for example on the surface of a bacterium, that the immune system recognises. Antibodies bind exactly to this feature.

111784.q: What shape are antibodies in simplified drawings?
111784.e: An antibody consists of four protein chains that together form a Y. The binding sites for the antigen are on the two arms.

111785.q: By which principle does an antibody fit its antigen?
111785.e: An antibody only fits one particular antigen, just as a key only fits one lock. That is why the defence is specific.
111785.m: Antibody and antigen fit like a key and a lock.

111786.q: Which T cells kill virus-infected body cells in a targeted way?
111786.e: Killer T cells, also called cytotoxic T cells, recognise infected cells by their antigens. Then they make them die.
111786.m: Killer T cells destroy infected body cells.

111787.q: What job do helper T cells do?
a: They activate and direct other defence cells
111787.e: Helper T cells release messenger substances that activate B cells and killer cells. They are something like the command centre of the defence.
111787.m: Helper T cells coordinate the specific defence.

111788.q: The first time you meet a germ, roughly how long does it take for the specific defence to work fully?
111788.e: First, matching lymphocytes have to be found, activated and multiplied. The first time, this takes about one to two weeks.
111788.m: The first specific defence needs a few days to weeks.

111789.q: What is the mucus on the linings of the airways for?
111789.e: Particles and germs that are breathed in stick in the sticky mucus. That way they do not get deeper into the lungs.
111789.m: Mucus traps germs in the airways.

111790.q: Which tiny hairs move mucus in the airways towards the throat?
111790.e: Cilia move like a waving carpet and push the mucus upwards. There it is swallowed or coughed up.
111790.m: Cilia carry mucus out of the airways.

111791.q: Which part of the body is lined inside with mucous membrane?
111791.e: Mucous membranes line inner cavities that are connected to the outside world, such as the nose, mouth and gut. Fingertips, soles of the feet and the scalp are covered by normal skin.
111791.m: The nose, mouth and gut are lined with mucous membrane.

111792.q: Which defence substances give the mucous membranes extra protection from germs?
111792.e: There are special antibodies in saliva, tears and gut mucus. They stop germs from settling on the mucous membranes.

111793.q: Which reflex shoots irritants and germs out of the nose?
111793.e: Irritation of the lining of the nose triggers a sneeze. Air is pushed out through the nose and mouth at high speed.
111793.m: Sneezing cleans irritants out of the nose.

111794.q: Which reflex clears mucus from the bronchi?
111794.e: When you cough, air is forced strongly out of the lungs. This carries mucus with germs out of the lower airways.
111794.m: Coughing clears mucus from the bronchi.

111795.q: What is an inflammation of the lining of the nose called in everyday language?
111795.e: With a runny nose, the lining of the nose is inflamed and makes a lot of mucus. Experts call this rhinitis.
111795.m: A runny nose is an inflammation of the lining of the nose.

111796.q: What protects the stomach lining from being attacked by its own acid?
111796.e: The stomach lining makes sticky mucus and bicarbonate. This layer keeps the acid away from the cells.
111796.m: Mucus protects the stomach from its own acid.

111797.q: What is the mucous membrane called that covers the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelids?
111797.e: The conjunctiva is a thin, see-through mucous membrane. If it is inflamed, this is called conjunctivitis.
111797.m: The conjunctiva is the mucous membrane of the eye.

111798.q: What is meant by herd immunity?
a: Protection of people who are not immune because many others are
Immunity that only occurs in farm animals
Protection from living in a big city
111798.e: If enough people are immune, a germ hardly finds any new chances to spread. That way people without their own protection are also protected indirectly.
111798.m: Herd immunity also protects people who are not immune themselves.

111799.q: Roughly how high must the share of immune people be for measles to create herd immunity?
111799.e: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases of all. That is why very high immunity is needed in the population, around 95 percent.
111799.m: Almost everyone has to be immune to measles.

111800.q: Why is an especially high share of immune people needed for measles?
a: Because there is no vaccine against measles
111800.e: Without immunity in the population, one person with measles can infect a great many others. The more contagious a disease is, the higher the threshold needed.
111800.m: The more contagious a disease, the more immune people are needed.

111801.q: A sick person infects 2 people, and each of them infects 2 more. How many people are infected in this second round?
111801.e: In the first round, 2 people are infected. Each of them infects 2 more: 2 times 2 makes 4. That is how a disease spreads very quickly without protection.
111801.m: Without protection, the number of sick people multiplies with every round.

111802.q: The threshold for herd immunity is calculated, in simplified form, as 1 minus 1/R0. What percentage do you get when R0 = 4?
111802.e: 1 minus 1/4 = 1 minus 0.25 = 0.75. So about 75 percent of the population must be immune.
111802.m: The bigger R0 is, the higher the threshold for herd immunity.

111803.q: Which disease was declared eradicated in 1980 thanks to worldwide vaccination programmes?
111803.e: The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980. So far it is the only human infectious disease to have been wiped out.
111803.m: Smallpox was wiped out by vaccination.

111804.q: What can happen if the vaccination rate falls below the necessary threshold?
a: The germ then dies out immediately
111804.e: If too few people are immune, the germ again finds enough chains of infection. Then a disease can spread again.
111804.m: If the vaccination rate falls, new outbreaks threaten.

111805.q: In a population with herd immunity, when does a disease start to decline?
a: When each sick person infects fewer than one person on average
When each sick person infects fewer than ten people on average
When each sick person infects fewer than five people on average
When each sick person infects fewer than a hundred people on average
111805.e: If each sick person infects fewer than one other person on average, the cases become fewer each time. The chains of infection then break off.
111805.m: A disease dies down when each sick person infects fewer than one other person.

111806.q: What is meant by the incubation period?
a: The time from infection to the first symptoms
The whole length of an illness
The time you spend in hospital
The time from the symptoms to recovery
111806.e: The incubation period starts when a germ gets into the body. It ends when the first signs of illness appear.
111806.m: The incubation period lies between infection and the start of illness.

111807.q: Roughly how long is the incubation period for chickenpox?
111807.e: With chickenpox, it usually takes around 14 to 16 days until the rash appears. The range is about 8 to 28 days.
111807.m: Chickenpox breaks out about two weeks after infection.

111808.q: How long is the incubation period for real flu usually?
111808.e: With influenza, the symptoms often start just one to two days after infection. That is why a flu wave can spread very quickly.
111808.m: Flu breaks out only a few days after infection.

111809.q: Why can diseases already spread during the incubation period?
a: Because you are sometimes contagious before you feel ill
Because germs grow through the air during this time
Because the body then has no defence cells
Because you always have a fever during this time
111809.e: With some diseases, you already give off germs before symptoms appear. You do not notice the infection yet and pass it on without knowing.
111809.m: Some sick people are contagious before they have symptoms.

111810.q: What happens in the body during the incubation period?
111810.e: In this phase, the germs multiply until there are enough of them to cause symptoms. At the same time, the immune system begins to react.
111810.m: During the incubation period, the germs multiply unnoticed.

111811.q: Which disease often has an especially long incubation period of several weeks to months?
111811.e: With rabies, the virus travels slowly along the nerves to the brain. That is why it usually takes weeks to months until the first symptoms appear.
111811.m: Rabies can stay unnoticed in the body for a very long time.

111812.q: With which illness do the symptoms often start just a few hours after infection?
111812.e: In food poisoning caused by bacterial toxins, the poisons act directly. That is why nausea and vomiting often start after just a few hours.
111812.m: Bacterial toxins in food act after just a few hours.

111813.q: With measles, roughly how long does it take from infection to the first signs of illness?
111813.e: With measles, the first symptoms such as fever and a runny nose usually appear about 8 to 10 days after infection. The typical rash follows a few days later.
111813.m: Measles begins about ten days after infection.

111814.q: With infectious diseases, what is the length of a quarantine often based on?
a: The weather over the next few days
The age of the person affected
The day of the week of the infection
111814.e: A quarantine should last until you can be sure that no illness will break out. That is why it is based on the incubation period.
111814.m: The length of a quarantine depends on the incubation period.

112108.e: Real flu, also called influenza, is caused by flu viruses. Cold alone does not make you ill.
112108.m: Real flu is caused by viruses.

a: A worldwide flu wave with millions of deaths
A harmless cold only in Spain
112109.e: The Spanish flu began in 1918 towards the end of the First World War. It spread across the whole world and killed many millions of people.
112109.m: The Spanish flu was a worldwide flu wave from 1918.

112110.q: In which season are there the most cases of flu in Switzerland?
112110.e: In Switzerland the flu wave usually reaches its peak between December and March. That is why people speak of the flu season in winter.
112110.m: In Switzerland, the flu season is in winter.

112111.q: What is typical of real flu compared with an ordinary cold?
112111.e: Real flu usually starts very suddenly with a high fever, aching limbs and a strong feeling of being ill. A cold, on the other hand, usually develops more slowly and is milder.
112111.m: Flu usually starts suddenly with a high fever.

112112.q: How are flu viruses mainly passed from person to person?
112112.e: When you cough, sneeze and talk, tiny droplets with viruses get into the air and others breathe them in. The viruses can also be passed on by hands.
112112.m: Flu is mainly passed on through droplets when coughing and sneezing.

112113.q: What is the form of influenza called that mainly affects birds?
112113.e: Bird flu is caused by certain influenza A viruses that mainly affect wild birds and poultry. People only rarely catch it.
112113.m: Bird flu is an influenza that mainly makes birds ill.

112114.q: What is a disease called that spreads across the whole world?
112114.e: A pandemic is a wave of disease that affects many countries and continents. Examples are the Spanish flu and COVID-19.
112114.m: A worldwide wave of disease is called a pandemic.

112115.q: Which kind of medicine works directly against flu viruses?
112115.e: Antiviral drugs slow down the multiplication of flu viruses in the body. They work best if you take them early after the illness starts.
112115.m: Antiviral drugs can slow down the multiplication of flu viruses.

112116.q: For which age group does the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) especially recommend the flu vaccination?
112116.e: Older people more often become seriously ill with flu. That is why the FOPH recommends the vaccination for everyone over 65 and for people with chronic illnesses, among others.
112116.m: From the age of 65, the flu vaccination is especially recommended.

112117.q: Which rare but very dangerous complication can measles cause?
112117.e: In rare cases, measles can cause an inflammation of the brain that can leave lasting damage or be fatal. Middle ear infections and pneumonia are more common.
112117.m: Measles can rarely cause a dangerous inflammation of the brain.

112118.q: Which sign of illness is typical of measles?
a: Red spots all over the body with a high fever
A ring around a tick bite
112118.e: With measles you get a high fever and a red, blotchy rash that usually starts behind the ears and spreads over the body.
112118.m: Measles shows itself with fever and red spots all over the body.

112119.q: What kind of vaccine is used against measles?
a: A live vaccine with weakened viruses
A vaccine made of killed bacteria
112119.e: The measles vaccine contains live but greatly weakened measles viruses. They do not make you ill, but they train the immune system.
112119.m: Measles vaccines use weakened, live viruses.

112120.q: Why could measles be wiped out worldwide?
a: Because the virus only occurs in humans
Because the virus only lives in winter
112120.e: The measles virus has no animal hosts. If enough people are vaccinated, it finds no new victims and disappears.
112120.m: Measles could be wiped out because only humans carry the virus.

112121.q: What does measles often do to the immune system for months to years?
a: It makes you immune to all diseases
112121.e: The measles virus destroys defence cells that remember earlier germs. Afterwards, people affected catch other infections more easily.
112121.m: Measles weakens the memory of the immune system.

112122.q: What do you typically see on the skin with chickenpox?
112122.e: Chickenpox is caused by a virus. Typical are itchy, fluid-filled blisters all over the body.
112122.m: Chickenpox causes itchy blisters on the skin.

112123.q: Where does the German name for chickenpox, “Windpocken” (wind pox), come from?
a: The viruses are spread far through the air
You only get them in a storm
They heal faster in the wind
112123.e: The name shows that the viruses can be carried several metres with the air we breathe out. So they spread, as it were, with the wind.
112123.m: In German, chickenpox is called wind pox because it spreads far through the air.

112124.q: Until when is a child with chickenpox contagious?
a: Until all the blisters have crusted over
112124.e: The fluid in the blisters contains many viruses. Only when all the blisters have dried up and crusted over are you no longer contagious.
112124.m: With chickenpox you are contagious until all the blisters have crusted over.

112125.q: What should you try not to do when you have chickenpox?
112125.e: Scratched blisters can become infected and leave scars. Short fingernails and cooling remedies for the itching help.
112125.m: You should not scratch chickenpox blisters.

112126.q: Who discovered the germ that causes tuberculosis in 1882?
112126.e: The German doctor Robert Koch presented his discovery in Berlin in 1882. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it in 1905.
112126.m: Robert Koch discovered the tuberculosis germ in 1882.

a: Yes, it is one of the most common deadly infectious diseases worldwide
No, it was wiped out 100 years ago
112127.e: Every year, millions of people worldwide fall ill with tuberculosis, mainly in poorer countries. In Switzerland it has become rare.

112128.q: Which organ does tuberculosis affect most often?
112128.e: Tuberculosis of the lungs is the most common. But the bacteria can also affect bones, lymph nodes or other organs.
112128.m: Tuberculosis most often affects the lungs.

112129.e: Against tuberculosis, several antibiotics are taken at the same time for at least six months. This stops the bacteria from becoming resistant.
112129.m: Tuberculosis is treated for months with several antibiotics.

112130.q: Which place in the Grisons became famous in the 19th century for its health resorts for people with lung disease?
112130.e: From about 1865, many sanatoriums were built in Davos because people believed the mountain air helped with tuberculosis. That is how the place became a well-known health resort.
112130.m: Davos became famous as a health resort for people with lung disease.

112131.q: What was tuberculosis commonly called in the past?
112131.e: Because the sick became very thin and slowly “wasted away”, people used to call it consumption.
112131.m: Tuberculosis used to be called consumption.

112132.q: Are all children in Switzerland vaccinated against tuberculosis today?
a: There is no vaccine against it at all
112132.e: There is a vaccine against tuberculosis, the BCG vaccine. Because the disease is rare in Switzerland, it is now only recommended in special cases.
112132.m: In Switzerland, people are only vaccinated against tuberculosis in special cases.

112133.q: How is tuberculosis usually passed on?
112133.e: People with active tuberculosis of the lungs cough bacteria into the air. Others breathe them in and can become infected.
112133.m: Tuberculosis is passed on through the air we breathe.

a: The bacteria do not respond to several antibiotics
The bacteria live in several countries
112134.e: With multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, the most important standard medicines no longer work. Treatment is then much longer and more difficult.
112134.m: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis cannot be cured with the usual antibiotics.

112135.q: Which animal passes malaria on to humans?
112135.e: Malaria is passed on by the bite of mosquitoes of the genus Anopheles. They take in the germs when sucking blood and pass them on.
112135.m: Malaria is passed on by Anopheles mosquitoes.

112136.q: What does the Italian expression “mala aria”, which malaria comes from, mean?
112136.e: People used to believe the disease came from bad air from swamps. That is where the name malaria comes from.

112137.q: Which Anopheles mosquitoes bite and pass on malaria?
112137.e: Only female mosquitoes suck blood, because they need it for their eggs to develop. Males feed on plant juices.
112137.m: Only female Anopheles mosquitoes pass on malaria.

112138.q: Which sign of illness is typical of malaria?
a: A red ring around the bite
Loss of the sense of smell
112138.e: With malaria, bouts of fever with shivering often occur at regular intervals. They happen when many infected blood cells burst at the same time.
112138.m: Malaria causes repeated attacks of fever.

112139.q: In which region of the world are there the most cases of malaria?
a: In Africa south of the Sahara
112139.e: Most malaria cases and deaths are in countries in Africa south of the Sahara. Young children are especially at risk.
112139.m: Most malaria cases are in Africa south of the Sahara.

112140.q: Which plant does the old malaria medicine quinine come from?
112140.e: Quinine is obtained from the bark of the cinchona tree from South America. For a long time it was the most important medicine against malaria.
112140.m: Quinine from cinchona bark was long the most important malaria medicine.

112141.q: Which simple item protects especially well against malaria at night?
a: A mosquito net over the bed
112141.e: Anopheles mosquitoes mainly bite at dusk and at night. A mosquito net treated with insecticide keeps them away from the sleeper.
112141.m: A mosquito net protects against malaria mosquitoes at night.

112142.q: In which blood cells do the malaria germs multiply?
a: In the blood plasma without cells
112142.e: After a phase in the liver, the plasmodia enter red blood cells, multiply there and make them burst.
112142.m: Malaria germs multiply in the red blood cells.

112143.q: What kind of germ causes malaria?
112143.e: Malaria is caused by tiny single-celled parasites called plasmodia. The mosquito passes them into the blood when it bites.
112143.m: Malaria is caused by single-celled parasites.

112144.q: What kind of germ causes cholera?
112144.e: Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae.
112144.m: Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae.

112145.q: What is the main feature of cholera?
112145.e: The toxin of the cholera bacteria causes very severe, watery diarrhoea in the gut. You can lose many litres of fluid a day.
112145.m: Cholera causes very severe, watery diarrhoea.

112146.q: How do people usually catch cholera?
112146.e: Cholera bacteria get into the water through the waste of sick people. Anyone who drinks contaminated water or eats food washed in it can become infected.
112146.m: Cholera mainly spreads through dirty water.

112147.q: In 1854 in London, how did a doctor find out that cholera came from the water of a pump?
a: He marked the cases of illness on a map of the city
He counted the rats in the streets
112147.e: The doctor John Snow marked all the cholera cases on a city map. They were clustered around a water pump in Broad Street.
112147.m: A city map with all the cases showed that cholera spreads through water.

112148.q: What is most important in treating cholera?
112148.e: The loss is made up with a drink made of water, sugar and salts, or with drips. That way almost everyone who is treated survives.
112148.m: With cholera, above all fluids and salts must be replaced.

112149.q: What do untreated cholera patients usually die of?
a: The body's huge loss of water
A heart attack caused by fever
112149.e: The diarrhoea dries out the body, the blood becomes thick and the circulation fails. Without treatment this can be fatal within hours.
112149.m: Cholera is dangerous because the body dries out.

112150.q: In the 19th century, which measure helped most against cholera in European cities?
112150.e: Once it was understood that the disease got into drinking water through sewage, many cities built sewers and safe water pipes. After that the outbreaks fell sharply.
112150.m: Sewers and clean water drove cholera out of Europe's cities.

112151.q: How is the cholera vaccine given?
a: As an oral vaccine you swallow
112151.e: The cholera vaccine is drunk so that it works directly in the gut, where the bacteria attack.
112151.m: There is an oral vaccine against cholera.

a: They are curved like a comma
112152.e: Vibrio cholerae is a slightly curved rod that looks like a comma. With a long whip-like tail it can move quickly.
112152.m: Cholera bacteria look like a comma.

112153.q: What is the virus called that causes COVID-19?
112153.e: COVID-19 is caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2. It is related to the SARS virus of 2002.
112153.m: COVID-19 is caused by the virus SARS-CoV-2.

112154.q: In which city was COVID-19 first detected at the end of 2019?
112154.e: The first cases of the new lung disease became known in December 2019 in Wuhan in China. From there the virus spread worldwide.
112154.m: COVID-19 was first discovered in Wuhan at the end of 2019.

112155.q: What does it mean that COVID-19 was a pandemic?
a: The disease spread across the whole world
The disease only existed in one village
The disease only occurred in summer
112155.e: A pandemic is a disease that spreads across many countries and continents. In March 2020, COVID-19 was officially declared a pandemic.
112155.m: A pandemic is the worldwide spread of a disease.

112156.q: What did the Federal Council close throughout Switzerland in March 2020 because of COVID-19?
112156.e: In March 2020 the Federal Council declared an extraordinary situation. Schools and many shops were closed; food shops and hospitals stayed open.
112156.m: In March 2020, schools in Switzerland were closed.

112157.q: Which variant of SARS-CoV-2 spread especially quickly worldwide from the end of 2021?
112157.e: The Omicron variant was first reported in November 2021 and within a few weeks pushed out the earlier variants. The WHO named the variants with Greek letters.
112157.m: From the end of 2021, the Omicron variant took over worldwide.

112158.q: Which document did adults in Switzerland have to show at times in 2021, for example to eat in a restaurant?
112158.e: The COVID certificate confirmed a vaccination, recovery or a negative test. It was shown as a QR code on a phone or on paper.
112158.m: The COVID certificate was required in many places in 2021.

112159.q: Which new vaccine technology was used on a large scale for the first time against COVID-19?
112159.e: mRNA vaccines contain a blueprint that body cells use to make a part of the virus. That way the immune system learns to recognise the real virus.
112159.m: mRNA vaccines were widely used for the first time against COVID-19.

112160.q: What does the number 19 in “COVID-19” stand for?
112160.e: COVID stands for “coronavirus disease”. The 19 shows that it was discovered in 2019.
112160.m: The number 19 in COVID-19 stands for the year it was discovered.

112161.e: “Corona” is Latin for crown or wreath. Under the electron microscope, the viruses have wreath-like spikes on their surface.
112161.m: Coronaviruses are named after their crown-like shape.

112162.q: Which rule applied on public transport in Switzerland from July 2020?
a: Wearing a bike helmet was compulsory
112162.e: From 6 July 2020, masks had to be worn on trains, trams and buses throughout Switzerland. Later the rule was extended to other places.
112162.m: From July 2020, masks were compulsory on public transport in Switzerland.

112163.q: What was the federal government's app called that warned of possible COVID infections?
112163.e: The SwissCovid app used Bluetooth to detect who had been close to a person who later tested positive for a long time. It was introduced in June 2020.
112163.m: The SwissCovid app warned of possible infections.

112164.q: What is another English name for tetanus?
112164.e: Tetanus is also called lockjaw, because the germs get in through wounds and cause strong muscle cramps, often starting in the jaw.

112165.q: Where are tetanus bacteria mainly found?
112165.e: The bacterium Clostridium tetani lives in soil, in dust and in the gut of animals. It is found practically everywhere.
112165.m: Tetanus germs live almost everywhere in the soil.

112166.q: Which sign is typical of tetanus?
a: A red ring on the skin
112166.e: Tetanus often starts with a locked jaw, so you can hardly open your mouth. Later, other muscles all over the body cramp up.
112166.m: Tetanus often starts with cramped jaw muscles.

112167.q: After a dirty wound, for example from a fall on soil, what should you check?
a: Whether your tetanus vaccination is still valid
Whether your blood group is right
Whether you are allergic to pollen
Whether you have had enough vitamin C
112167.e: Tetanus germs get into the body through dirty wounds. That is why you should look in your vaccination record to see whether you need a booster.
112167.m: After dirty wounds, you check your tetanus protection.

112168.q: Can you catch tetanus from a person who has it?
112168.e: Tetanus is not passed from person to person. You only catch it through dirty wounds, so only your own vaccination protects you.
112168.m: Tetanus is not contagious from person to person.

112169.q: What causes the cramps in tetanus?
a: A poison made by the bacteria
Too much sugar in the blood
112169.e: The bacteria make a strong nerve poison called tetanospasmin. It disturbs the control of the muscles, which then cramp up all the time.
112169.m: A nerve poison from tetanus bacteria causes the cramps.

112170.q: In what form do tetanus germs survive in the soil for years?
112170.e: The bacteria form very tough spores that can withstand heat and drought for a long time. In a wound they start to grow again.
112170.m: Tetanus germs survive in the soil as spores.

112171.q: Together with which other disease is the tetanus vaccine usually given to adults?
112171.e: In Switzerland, the tetanus vaccine is usually given as a combined vaccine with diphtheria, often also with whooping cough.
112171.m: Tetanus is usually vaccinated against together with diphtheria.

112172.q: Are you immune after you have recovered from tetanus?
a: No, you still need to be vaccinated
112172.e: Even a tiny amount of tetanus poison is enough to cause the disease, but too little to build up protection. That is why you need a vaccination even after the illness.
112172.m: After tetanus you are not immune and need a vaccination.

112173.q: What kind of germ causes Lyme disease?
112173.e: The germs that cause Lyme disease are corkscrew-shaped bacteria called Borrelia. That is why the disease can be treated with antibiotics.
112173.m: Lyme disease is caused by bacteria called Borrelia.

112174.e: Because Borrelia are bacteria, the disease is treated with antibiotics. The earlier treatment starts, the better.
112174.m: Lyme disease is treated with antibiotics.

112175.q: Why should you remove a tick as quickly as possible?
a: Because Borrelia are usually only passed on after hours
Because otherwise the tick lays eggs in the skin
Because otherwise it moves into the body
112175.e: The Borrelia sit in the tick's gut and usually only get into the skin after many hours of sucking. Removing the tick quickly lowers the risk a lot.
112175.m: A tick that is removed quickly passes on Lyme disease less often.

112176.q: Which place is Lyme disease named after?
112176.e: In the 1970s, a cluster of joint inflammation in children was noticed in the area around Lyme in the US state of Connecticut. The disease was named after it.
112176.m: Lyme disease is named after the town of Lyme in the USA.

112177.q: Where in Switzerland can you catch Lyme disease?
112177.e: Ticks carrying Borrelia are found throughout Switzerland, especially in woods, at the edges of woods and in long grass, up to medium altitudes.
112177.m: You can catch Lyme disease almost anywhere in Switzerland.

112178.q: Which long-term effect can untreated Lyme disease have?
112178.e: If the infection is not treated, joints, especially the knees, can swell months later. Nerves and the heart can also be affected.
112178.m: Untreated Lyme disease can lead to inflamed joints.

112179.q: Which group of animals do ticks belong to?
112179.e: Like mites, ticks belong to the arachnids and not to the insects, even though they are often thought to be insects.

112180.q: As of 2025, was there an approved vaccine against Lyme disease for humans in Switzerland?
a: No, you mainly protect yourself against tick bites
Yes, it is compulsory for all children
Yes, it is in the basic vaccination plan
Yes, it is given together with measles
112180.e: Unlike for TBE, there was no approved vaccine against Lyme disease for humans. That is why long clothes, tick repellent and checking your body after being outdoors are important.
112180.m: Protection against tick bites is the main help against Lyme disease.

112181.q: What kind of germ causes TBE (tick-borne encephalitis)?
112181.e: TBE is caused by the TBE virus, which belongs to the flavivirus family. That is why antibiotics do not work against it.
112181.m: TBE is caused by a virus.

112182.q: For which areas does the FOPH recommend the TBE vaccination (as of 2025)?
a: For the whole of Switzerland except Ticino
Only for the canton of Zurich
112182.e: According to the FOPH, as of 2025 the whole of Switzerland except the canton of Ticino counts as a TBE risk area. The vaccination is recommended for anyone who spends time outdoors there.
112182.m: The TBE vaccination is recommended for almost the whole of Switzerland.

112183.q: What does the German abbreviation FSME, used for tick-borne encephalitis, stand for?
112183.e: In German the disease is called early-summer meningoencephalitis, because ticks are especially active from early summer and the virus can inflame the membranes around the brain and the brain itself.

112184.q: Which parts of the body can TBE inflame?
a: The membranes around the brain and the brain
112184.e: Meningitis means inflammation of the membranes around the brain; encephalitis means inflammation of the brain. In severe cases, lasting paralysis can result.
112184.m: TBE can inflame the brain and the membranes around it.

112185.q: Which statement about the treatment of TBE is true?
a: There is no medicine against the virus
112185.e: There is no effective medicine against the TBE virus itself; only the symptoms can be eased. That is why vaccination is the most important protection.
112185.m: Vaccination is the main protection against TBE, because it cannot be cured.

112186.q: What is the best way to protect yourself from TBE?
112186.e: There is no medicine against the TBE virus. Vaccination and long clothes in the woods protect best.

112187.q: Through which food can TBE also be passed on in rare cases?
112187.e: Goats, sheep or cows that have been bitten by infected ticks can pass the virus out in their milk. Heating kills it.
112187.m: Unpasteurised raw milk can rarely pass on TBE.

112188.q: Which animal usually passes the TBE virus on to humans?
112188.e: TBE is almost always passed on by tick bites. That is why you should check yourself for ticks after a trip to the woods.

112189.q: What is meant by a pandemic?
a: A disease in a single village
112189.e: In a pandemic, an infectious disease spreads across countries and continents. So it affects a great many people all over the world.
112189.m: A pandemic is a worldwide epidemic.

112190.q: What does the Greek prefix “pan” in the word pandemic mean?
112190.e: “Pan” means all or whole, and “demos” means people. So a pandemic affects, as it were, all the people.

112191.q: Which disease caused the “Black Death” in Europe in the 14th century?
112191.e: From 1347, the plague spread across Europe and killed an estimated third of the population. It is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
112191.m: The Black Death in the 14th century was the plague.

112192.q: Which organisation officially determines whether there is a pandemic?
112192.e: The World Health Organization (WHO) monitors the spread of diseases worldwide and can declare a pandemic.
112192.m: The WHO officially declares a pandemic.

112193.q: In which Swiss city does the World Health Organization have its headquarters?
112193.e: The World Health Organization was founded in 1948 and has its headquarters on Lake Geneva. Many international organisations are based there.
112193.m: The World Health Organization has its headquarters in Geneva.

112194.q: Why can diseases spread around the world faster today than in the past?
112194.e: By plane, infected people can reach other continents within a few hours. In the past, such journeys took weeks.
112194.m: Air travel lets diseases travel quickly around the world today.

112195.q: What does “flattening the curve” mean in a pandemic?
a: Spreading infections out over time so hospitals are not overwhelmed
112195.e: When fewer people are infected at the same time, the sick are spread over a longer period. That way hospitals have enough beds for everyone.
112195.m: A flat curve protects hospitals from being overwhelmed.

112196.q: Which animals mainly spread the plague?
112196.e: Plague bacteria live in rodents such as rats. When their host dies, rat fleas also bite people and pass on the disease.
112196.m: The plague was mainly spread by rat fleas.

112197.q: Why is the Spanish flu called that, even though it did not start in Spain?
a: Because Spanish newspapers were the first to report on it openly
Because a Spaniard discovered the virus
Because it came with Spanish fruit
112197.e: Spain was neutral in the First World War and did not censor its press. So the first open reports appeared there, and the epidemic got its name.
112197.m: The Spanish flu is named after the first open reports from Spain.

112198.q: Which federal office leads the measures against a pandemic in Switzerland?
a: The Federal Office of Public Health
112198.e: The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) monitors infectious diseases and has drawn up a pandemic plan for Switzerland.
112198.m: In Switzerland, the FOPH is responsible for fighting pandemics.

a: A large number of cases of a disease in a particular area and period
A disease that only one single person has
112199.e: In an epidemic, many more people than usual in a region fall ill within a short time. It is limited to one area.
112199.m: An epidemic is a disease concentrated in one place and time.

112201.q: Which federal law governs the fight against infectious diseases in Switzerland?
112201.e: The Epidemics Act sets out how the Confederation and the cantons detect, monitor and fight infectious diseases. The current version has been in force since 2016.
112201.m: In Switzerland, the Epidemics Act governs how epidemics are handled.

112202.q: What does a reproduction number R above 1 mean?
a: The number of infections is rising
The disease has been wiped out
Nobody is being infected any more
The number of cases stays exactly the same
112202.e: R tells you how many people one sick person infects on average. If R is greater than 1, each person infects more than one other and cases increase.
112202.m: With a reproduction number above 1, a disease spreads.

112203.q: One person infects 3 others, and each of them infects 3 more. How many new infections are there in this second round?
112203.e: In the first round, 3 people are infected. Each of them infects 3 more, so 3 times 3 equals 9.
112203.m: Infections grow from round to round by multiplying.

112204.q: In which region was there a large Ebola epidemic from 2014 to 2016?
112204.e: The Ebola epidemic mainly affected Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia. It was the largest Ebola outbreak up to that time.
112204.m: The large Ebola epidemic of 2014 to 2016 hit West Africa.

112205.q: What is the science that studies how diseases spread in a population called?
112205.e: Epidemiology studies how often diseases occur, who is affected and what causes them.
112205.m: Epidemiology studies the spread of diseases.

112206.q: Who must doctors in Switzerland report certain infectious diseases to?
a: The cantonal and federal health authorities
112206.e: Many infectious diseases must be reported. This allows the cantonal doctor and the FOPH to detect outbreaks early and take action.
112206.m: Notifiable infectious diseases are reported to the health authorities.

112401.q: Which eye problem often occurs with a pollen allergy?
112401.e: Pollen lands on the conjunctiva of the eyes. In people with allergies it becomes inflamed, and the eyes turn red, itch and water.
112401.m: With a pollen allergy, the conjunctiva of the eyes often becomes inflamed.

112402.q: Why is a close-fitting pair of sunglasses useful for people with a pollen allergy when cycling?
a: They keep pollen away from the eyes
They filter pollen out of the air you breathe
112402.e: When cycling, lots of pollen flies straight into your face. Close-fitting glasses keep some of it away from the sensitive eyes.
112402.m: Glasses protect the eyes of people with pollen allergies from pollen.

112403.q: What do you call a substance that triggers an allergy?
112403.e: An allergen is a substance, usually containing protein, that the immune system reacts to allergically, for example a pollen grain or a food.
112403.m: A substance that triggers an allergy is called an allergen.

112404.q: Which symptoms are typical of a pollen allergy?
a: Sneezing, a runny nose and itchy eyes
112404.e: Pollen mainly irritates the mucous membranes of the nose and eyes. That is why sufferers often sneeze, have a runny nose and itchy, watery eyes.
112404.m: Hay fever mainly shows up in the nose and eyes.

112405.q: Why do plants with large, colourful flowers such as roses rarely cause hay fever?
a: Their pollen is carried by insects, not by the wind
Their pollen is smaller than dust
They produce no pollen at all
112405.e: Insect-pollinated plants have heavy, sticky pollen that hardly gets into the air. Hay fever is mainly caused by wind-pollinated plants such as grasses and many trees.
112405.m: Hay fever mainly comes from wind-pollinated plants.

112406.q: How can a pollen allergy be weakened in a targeted way over several years?
a: With regular small amounts of the allergen
With lots of sport when pollen counts are high
112406.e: In this treatment you receive small amounts of the allergen over several years. The immune system gets used to it and reacts less strongly.
112406.m: Small amounts of the allergen can get the body used to pollen.

112407.q: What can happen if hay fever is not treated for years?
a: The allergy can spread to the lungs and cause asthma
112407.e: Without treatment, the symptoms can move from the nose into the bronchial tubes. Allergic asthma can develop.
112407.m: Untreated hay fever can lead to asthma.

112408.q: Roughly what share of the Swiss population suffers from a pollen allergy?
112408.e: According to the Swiss Allergy Centre (aha!), around 20 per cent of the population suffer from a pollen allergy. This makes it one of the most common allergies.
112408.m: About one person in five in Switzerland has a pollen allergy.

112409.q: Which group of animals do house dust mites belong to?
112409.e: Like spiders, mites have eight legs, so they belong to the arachnids. Insects, on the other hand, have six legs.
112409.m: House dust mites are tiny arachnids with eight legs.

112410.q: What do house dust mites mainly feed on?
112410.e: People lose tiny flakes of skin every day. House dust mites live on these, especially where we spend a lot of time.
112410.m: House dust mites eat our flakes of skin.

112411.q: What mainly causes the symptoms of a house dust mite allergy?
112411.e: The allergens are mainly found in the mites’ tiny droppings. These break down into fine dust, which is breathed in.
112411.m: With a mite allergy, you mainly react to mite droppings.

112412.q: Where in a home do particularly large numbers of house dust mites live?
112412.e: In bed, mites find warmth, moisture from sweating and lots of skin flakes. That is why so many live there.
112412.m: Most house dust mites live in the bed.

112413.q: Which indoor climate do house dust mites particularly like?
112413.e: Mites thrive at room temperature and high humidity. They take in moisture directly from the air.
112413.m: House dust mites love warm, humid air.

112414.q: Why is a vacuum cleaner with a HEPA filter useful for people with a mite allergy?
a: It kills the mites with electricity
It makes the air more humid
112414.e: Ordinary vacuum cleaners blow some fine mite droppings back into the air. A HEPA filter traps even very small particles.
112414.m: A HEPA filter stops allergens being stirred up when vacuuming.

112415.q: When are the symptoms of a house dust mite allergy usually at their worst?
a: At night and in the morning after getting up
Only in spring when it is sunny
112415.e: In bed you breathe in mite allergens for hours. That is why a blocked nose and sneezing are usually worst at night and in the morning.
112415.m: A mite allergy is especially troublesome at night and in the morning.

112416.q: Which measure helps with a house dust mite allergy?
a: Mite-proof covers for the mattress and pillow
Lots of cuddly toys in bed
112416.e: Special mite-proof covers (encasings) keep the allergens inside the mattress. It also helps to wash bedding at a high temperature and air the room well.
112416.m: Mite-proof covers protect against mite allergens in bed.

112417.q: Can you see house dust mites with the naked eye?
a: Yes, they are as big as ants
Yes, they are as big as ladybirds
Yes, they are as big as houseflies
112417.e: House dust mites are usually only about a third of a millimetre long. You can only see them under a microscope or a strong magnifying glass.
112417.m: House dust mites cannot be seen with the naked eye.

112418.q: How must peanuts appear in the ingredients list of a food in Switzerland?
a: Not at all if there is only a little
112418.e: Peanuts are one of the main allergens. These must be clearly highlighted in the ingredients list, for example in bold, so that people with allergies can find them quickly.
112418.m: Main allergens such as peanuts are highlighted in the ingredients list.

112419.q: Which treatment can reduce some children’s sensitivity to peanuts under medical supervision?
a: Tiny, slowly increasing amounts of peanut protein
112419.e: In oral immunotherapy, the child receives a tiny amount of peanut protein every day, which is slowly increased. This may only be done under medical supervision, because reactions are possible.
112419.m: A peanut allergy may only be treated under medical supervision.

112420.q: What does the label “May contain traces of peanuts” on a packet mean?
a: Small amounts may get in during production
The product has been tested as peanut-free
112420.e: Peanuts are not an ingredient, but they are processed in the same factory. For people with a strong allergy, even this small amount can be dangerous.
112420.m: A traces warning warns of small, unintended amounts of an allergen.

112421.q: Why is a peanut allergy particularly feared?
a: Even tiny amounts can cause severe reactions
It only causes a mild skin rash
It only occurs in older people
It is contagious from person to person
112421.e: With a peanut allergy, even traces can trigger a life-threatening reaction. It is one of the most common causes of serious food allergy emergencies.
112421.m: With a peanut allergy, even traces can be dangerous.

112422.q: Does a peanut allergy usually go away by itself over time?
a: No, for most people it lasts a lifetime
Yes, almost always by the time children start school
Yes, if you eat peanuts every day
112422.e: Only a small number of children grow out of a peanut allergy. For most people affected, it lasts a lifetime.
112422.m: A peanut allergy usually lasts for life.

112423.q: Which group of plants does the peanut actually belong to?
112423.e: The peanut is not a real nut but a legume, like peas and beans. Its fruits ripen in the ground.

112424.q: Which dish particularly often contains peanuts?
112424.e: Satay sauce is made from ground peanuts. Peanuts can also be hidden in Asian dishes and muesli bars.

112425.q: Which protein from cereals triggers coeliac disease?
112425.e: In coeliac disease, the body cannot tolerate the cereal protein gluten. Casein, on the other hand, comes from milk, albumin from egg white and keratin from hair and nails.
112425.m: Coeliac disease is triggered by gluten.

112426.e: Gluten is found in wheat, rye and barley, for example. Rice, maize and millet are naturally gluten-free.

112427.q: Which organ is mainly damaged by coeliac disease?
112427.e: In coeliac disease, gluten makes the lining of the small intestine inflamed. As a result, the body absorbs nutrients less well.
112427.m: Coeliac disease damages the small intestine.

112428.q: Which cereal must people with coeliac disease also avoid?
112428.e: Spelt is closely related to wheat and also contains gluten. Despite its name, buckwheat is not wheat and is gluten-free.

a: With an operation on the intestine
112429.e: There is no medicine that cures coeliac disease. People who stick strictly to a gluten-free diet usually have no more symptoms, and the intestine recovers.
112429.m: With coeliac disease you must eat gluten-free all your life.

112430.q: Which side dish is naturally gluten-free?
112430.e: Potatoes contain no gluten. Spaghetti, couscous and bulgur, on the other hand, are made from wheat.

112431.q: Which symbol often marks gluten-free foods?
112431.e: The crossed-out ear of grain shows that a product is gluten-free. It helps people with coeliac disease when shopping.
112431.m: The crossed-out ear of grain means gluten-free.

112432.q: What happens in the body of someone with coeliac disease when they eat gluten?
a: The body’s defences attack the lining of the intestine
The body suddenly lacks vitamin C
112432.e: In coeliac disease, the body’s defences react wrongly to gluten and turn against the body’s own intestinal lining. So coeliac disease is not an infection and not poisoning.
112432.m: In coeliac disease, the body’s defences attack the intestine because of gluten.

112433.q: Roughly how many people have coeliac disease?
112433.e: Estimates suggest that around one per cent of the population have coeliac disease. Many do not know it, because the symptoms vary a great deal.
112433.m: About one per cent of people have coeliac disease.

a: A reaction to similar proteins in different substances
An allergy to plants with cross-shaped flowers
An allergy that only lasts two days
112434.e: In a cross-allergy, the immune system reacts to another substance because its proteins resemble the original allergen. This way, a pollen allergy can also cause reactions to foods.
112434.m: In a cross-allergy, the immune system confuses similar proteins.

112435.q: Which fruit do people with a birch pollen allergy particularly often react to?
112435.e: A protein in apples is very similar to the main allergen in birch pollen. That is why many people with a birch pollen allergy feel a tingling in the mouth when eating raw apples.
112435.m: People with a birch pollen allergy often cannot tolerate raw apples well.

112436.q: Which nut often causes a cross-reaction in people with a birch pollen allergy?
112436.e: Hazel and birch are closely related, and their proteins are similar. That is why people with a birch pollen allergy often also react to hazelnuts.
112436.m: The hazelnut is a cross-allergen that goes with birch.

112437.q: Which symptom is typical when people with a pollen allergy eat a cross-reacting fruit?
a: Tingling and itching in the mouth
Hair loss at the back of the head
112437.e: In what is called oral allergy syndrome, the lips, tongue and palate itch or tingle shortly after eating. Sometimes the lining of the mouth swells slightly.
112437.m: Cross-allergies to fruit often show up as itching in the mouth.

112438.q: Why can many people with a birch pollen allergy eat cooked apple purée but not a raw apple?
a: The protein causing the reaction is destroyed by heat
112438.e: The apple allergen that resembles the birch pollen allergen is sensitive to heat. When cooked or baked, it changes shape and the immune system no longer recognises it.
112438.m: Heat makes many fruit allergens harmless.

112439.q: Which fruit do people with a latex allergy often react to as well?
112439.e: In latex-fruit syndrome, people allergic to latex also react to fruits such as banana, avocado or kiwi. The reason is similar proteins.
112439.m: A latex allergy can be linked to a banana allergy.

112440.q: Which vegetable often causes a cross-reaction in people with a mugwort pollen allergy?
112440.e: Mugwort and celery have similar proteins. This is called celery-mugwort-spice syndrome, because spices can also be affected.
112440.m: Mugwort pollen and celery are a typical cross-allergy pair.

112441.q: Which foods can people with a house dust mite allergy react to because of a cross-allergy?
112441.e: Mites and crustaceans are both arthropods and have a similar muscle protein called tropomyosin. That is why cross-reactions are possible.
112441.m: A mite allergy and a crustacean allergy can be linked.

112442.q: Why should fresh fish always be kept well chilled?
a: Otherwise bacteria produce harmful substances such as histamine
Otherwise it becomes too hard to fry
112442.e: When it is warm, bacteria multiply in the fish. In doing so they produce histamine, which can cause flushing, headaches and nausea after eating.
112442.m: Poorly chilled fish can contain a lot of histamine.

112443.q: When does the body release a particularly large amount of histamine?
112443.e: When the immune system recognises an allergy trigger such as pollen, certain cells suddenly release histamine. This leads to sneezing, itching and swelling.
112443.m: In allergies, the body releases a lot of histamine.

112444.q: What effect does released histamine have in the skin?
112444.e: Histamine widens the blood vessels and makes them leakier. The skin turns red, swells and itches, as after a mosquito bite.
112444.m: Histamine makes the skin itch and swell.

112445.q: What are medicines that block the effect of histamine called?
112445.e: Antihistamines occupy the docking sites for histamine. In this way they relieve sneezing, itching and watery eyes.
112445.m: Antihistamines block the effect of histamine.

112446.q: Why do older allergy medicines against histamine often make you tired?
a: Histamine keeps you awake in the brain
They contain a lot of alcohol
112446.e: In the brain, histamine acts as a messenger for wakefulness. Older medicines reach the brain and block this effect there; newer ones hardly do.
112446.m: In the brain, histamine keeps you awake.

112447.q: From which amino acid does the body make histamine?
112447.e: Histamine is made from the amino acid histidine by removing a small chemical group. That is why the names of the two substances are almost the same.
112447.m: Histamine is made from the amino acid histidine.

112448.q: Which food contains a particularly large amount of histamine?
112448.e: During long maturing, microorganisms produce histamine. People with histamine intolerance therefore often do not tolerate matured cheese well.
112448.m: Long-matured foods contain a lot of histamine.

112449.q: What is it called when someone does not tolerate histamine from food well?
112449.e: With histamine intolerance, the intestine breaks down too little histamine from food. After cheese, wine or sauerkraut, symptoms can then occur.
112449.m: Someone who tolerates histamine poorly has histamine intolerance.

112450.q: Which fermented vegetable is particularly rich in histamine?
112450.e: Sauerkraut is made by fermentation with lactic acid bacteria. This produces a lot of histamine, whereas fresh vegetables contain hardly any.
112450.m: Sauerkraut contains a lot of histamine because of fermentation.

112451.q: What most often triggers anaphylaxis in children?
112451.e: In children, foods such as peanuts, nuts, milk and egg are the most common triggers. In adults, insect stings and medicines play a bigger role.
112451.m: In children, anaphylaxis is usually triggered by foods.

112452.q: Which existing illness makes anaphylaxis particularly dangerous?
112452.e: With asthma, the airways are already sensitive. If they also swell up during anaphylaxis, severe breathing difficulties can quickly follow.
112452.m: Asthma increases the risk of severe anaphylaxis.

112453.q: What happens to blood pressure during anaphylactic shock?
112453.e: Many messenger substances such as histamine suddenly widen the blood vessels. As a result, blood pressure falls and organs get too little blood.
112453.m: During anaphylaxis, blood pressure drops dangerously.

112454.q: Which sign points to dangerous anaphylaxis?
112454.e: If the throat or airways swell, the person cannot breathe properly. This is a warning sign of a severe allergic reaction.
112454.m: Breathlessness after contact with an allergen is a warning sign.

112455.q: How quickly does anaphylaxis usually develop?
112455.e: Anaphylaxis usually begins a few minutes to about an hour after contact with the allergen. That is why you must act quickly.

112456.q: How should you position a person with anaphylaxis who mainly has circulation problems but is breathing well?
a: Lying flat with the legs raised
Lying on their front with the head down
112456.e: With circulation problems, raising the legs helps more blood flow to the heart and brain. If the person is short of breath, however, let them sit upright.
112456.m: With circulation problems, raise the legs.

112457.q: Why must you go to hospital after anaphylaxis, even if you are already feeling better?
a: The reaction can come back hours later
Only there can you collect your emergency card
The health insurer requires a report
There you are immediately vaccinated against the allergy
112457.e: After anaphylaxis, a second wave of reaction can follow, even if you feel better at first. That is why you are monitored in hospital for a few hours.
112457.m: After anaphylaxis, you belong in hospital for monitoring.

112458.q: Which skin signs often appear during anaphylaxis?
a: Itchy weals like after stinging nettles
112458.e: Itchy, raised weals often appear all over the body. They are often the first visible sign.
112458.m: Weals all over the body can signal anaphylaxis.

112459.q: Where do you inject an adrenaline auto-injector in an emergency?
a: Into the outer side of the thigh
Into the tummy next to the belly button
Into the inner side of the upper arm
Into the palm of the hand
112459.e: The large muscle on the outer side of the thigh absorbs the adrenaline quickly. You press the injector firmly there until it fires.
112459.m: You place the adrenaline auto-injector on the outer thigh.

112460.q: Can you inject an adrenaline auto-injector through trousers?
a: Yes, that is allowed in an emergency
No, the skin must be disinfected first
112460.e: The needle goes through normal clothing. That way no time is lost undressing in an emergency.
112460.m: An adrenaline auto-injector can be used through clothing.

112461.q: What does adrenaline do during a severe allergic reaction?
a: It makes breathing easier and supports the circulation
It makes you tired and sleepy
It makes blood pressure drop further
It cures the allergy for ever
112461.e: Adrenaline widens the airways and raises the dangerously low blood pressure again. But the allergy itself does not go away.
112461.m: Adrenaline supports the circulation and opens the airways.

112462.q: What should a child with a severe allergy always have with them?
a: Their emergency kit with the adrenaline auto-injector
112462.e: In a severe allergic reaction, every minute counts. That is why people with allergies always carry their emergency kit with the adrenaline auto-injector.
112462.m: People with allergies always carry their emergency kit.

112463.q: What do you do if the liquid in the viewing window of an adrenaline auto-injector is discoloured or cloudy?
a: Warm it up in the oven
112463.e: Normally the adrenaline solution is clear and colourless. If it is brownish or cloudy, the active ingredient has broken down and the device must be replaced.
112463.m: A discoloured adrenaline solution must be replaced.

112464.q: What must you check regularly on an adrenaline auto-injector?
112464.e: Adrenaline only keeps for a limited time. An expired auto-injector may work less well and should be replaced.
112464.m: Check the expiry date of the emergency kit regularly.

112465.q: How should you store an adrenaline auto-injector correctly?
a: In a hot car in the sun
112465.e: Adrenaline is sensitive to heat and cold. Store the auto-injector at room temperature and always carry it with you.
112465.m: The adrenaline auto-injector must not be kept in heat or cold.

112466.q: What determines which dose an adrenaline auto-injector contains?
112466.e: For smaller children, there are auto-injectors with less adrenaline than for adults. The doctor chooses the dose according to body weight.
112466.m: The adrenaline dose depends on body weight.

112467.q: When should you use the adrenaline auto-injector if there are signs of a severe allergy?
a: Only once the person is unconscious
Only after phoning the family doctor
112467.e: Adrenaline works best when it is given early. Waiting too long is more dangerous than an injection that later turns out to have been unnecessary.
112467.m: In a severe allergic reaction, give adrenaline early.

112468.q: What is a classic measuring device called that draws in air and collects the pollen in it on a sticky strip?
112468.e: The pollen trap draws in air continuously, and the pollen sticks to a sticky strip. Experts then identify and count it under the microscope.
112468.m: A pollen trap measures how much pollen is in the air.

112469.q: In which months does grass pollen mainly fly in Switzerland?
112469.e: Grasses mainly flower in late spring and early summer. Most people with pollen allergies suffer most at this time.
112469.m: Grass pollen mainly flies in early summer.

112470.q: Which introduced plant causes strong pollen allergies in late summer and should be controlled?
112470.e: Ragweed comes from North America and flowers from about August to October. Its pollen is highly allergenic, which is why it is strictly controlled in Switzerland.
112470.m: The introduced ragweed is a strong allergy trigger.

112471.q: How does prolonged rain affect the amount of pollen in the air?
a: It washes the pollen out of the air
It doubles the amount of pollen
112471.e: Rain binds the pollen and brings it to the ground. After heavy rain, the air therefore often contains much less pollen.
112471.m: Rain cleans pollen out of the air.

112472.q: Why is the pollen load usually lower in the mountains?
a: Fewer plants flower there, and later
112472.e: At higher altitudes, plants are sparser and flowering starts later. That is why many people with allergies feel better in the mountains.
112472.m: In the mountains, the pollen load is usually lower.

112473.q: Why can the start of a thunderstorm be particularly unpleasant for people with a pollen allergy?
a: Pollen grains burst and break into tiny particles
The thunder irritates the lining of the nose
The pollen becomes bigger and heavier
112473.e: Moisture makes pollen grains burst, and strong gusts of wind spread the tiny fragments. These get deep into the airways and can trigger asthma attacks; this is called thunderstorm asthma.
112473.m: At the start of a thunderstorm, burst pollen can trigger asthma.

112474.q: In which unit is the pollen concentration in the air given?
a: Pollen per cubic metre of air
112474.e: The pollen concentration tells you how many pollen grains are floating in one cubic metre of air. The higher the value, the more people with allergies suffer.
112474.m: Pollen concentration is measured in pollen per cubic metre of air.

112475.q: How is climate change altering the pollen season in Switzerland?
a: It starts earlier and lasts longer
It starts later and is shorter
In some years it does not happen at all
It only takes place in winter
112475.e: Warmer temperatures make many plants flower earlier. Measurements by MeteoSwiss show that the pollen season starts earlier for several species.
112475.m: Because of global warming, the pollen season starts earlier.

112476.q: Which insects most often cause an insect venom allergy in Switzerland?
112476.e: Bees and wasps inject venom when they sting. Some people react allergically to it, up to life-threatening shock.
112476.m: Bees and wasps are the main causes of insect venom allergies.

112477.q: What usually happens to a honeybee after it has stung a person?
a: It sleeps for a whole day
It immediately grows a new sting
112477.e: The honeybee’s sting has barbs and stays stuck in the skin. When the bee flies away, the sting tears off together with the venom sac, and the bee dies.
112477.m: A honeybee usually dies after stinging the skin.

112478.q: Why can a wasp sting several times in a row?
a: Its sting is smooth and does not get stuck
It carries a lot of venom in its head
112478.e: The wasp’s sting has hardly any barbs. So the wasp can pull it out again and sting again.

112479.q: Is the saying true that a few hornet stings can kill a horse?
a: No, a hornet sting is hardly more dangerous than a wasp sting
112479.e: A hornet’s venom is no stronger per sting than a wasp’s. A sting is mainly dangerous with an allergy or with a very large number of stings.
112479.m: For healthy people, a hornet sting is no more dangerous than a wasp sting.

112480.q: Why is a wasp sting in the mouth dangerous even without an allergy?
a: The swelling can narrow the airways
The venom goes straight to the brain
You lose your sense of taste
112480.e: If the tongue or throat swells badly, it can become hard to breathe. That is why a sting in the mouth or throat must always be taken seriously.
112480.m: A sting in the mouth can be dangerous because of the swelling.

112481.q: What helps as a first measure after an insect sting in the mouth?
a: Sucking ice or drinking something cold
112481.e: Cold slows down the swelling in the mouth and throat. At the same time, if there are breathing problems, you should call the emergency number at once.
112481.m: After a sting in the mouth, cold helps against the swelling.

112482.q: In which season are wasps particularly common and pushy?
112482.e: In late summer, wasp colonies are at their largest. The insects then search more for sweet food, drinks and meat.
112482.m: In late summer there are particularly many wasps.

112483.q: Why should people with a bee venom allergy not walk barefoot across flowering meadows in summer?
a: They might step on a bee
The grass is particularly sharp then
Pollen gets in through the sole of the foot
112483.e: Bees collect nectar from clover and other low flowers. If you step on one barefoot, the bee stings to defend itself.
112483.m: Walking barefoot across flower meadows can lead to bee stings.

112484.q: What is the most common skin test for detecting allergies such as hay fever called?
112484.e: In the skin prick test, the skin is pricked lightly through drops containing allergens. If you are allergic, a skin reaction appears after a short time.
112484.m: The skin prick test is the most important skin test for allergies.

112485.q: On which part of the body is a skin prick test usually done?
a: On the inside of the forearm
On the sole of the foot
112485.e: The inside of the forearm is easy to reach and the skin there is thin. Sometimes the test is also done on the back.
112485.m: The skin prick test is usually done on the forearm.

112486.q: After how long is a skin prick test read?
112486.e: Immediate-type allergies show up quickly. After about a quarter of an hour, the specialist measures the size of the skin reaction.
112486.m: A skin prick test is read after about a quarter of an hour.

112487.q: How can you recognise a positive reaction in a skin prick test?
112487.e: With an allergy, a raised, itchy weal with a red ring forms at the test site. The bigger it is, the stronger the sensitisation.
112487.m: An itchy weal in a skin prick test indicates an allergy.

112488.q: Why are several substances tested at the same time in a skin prick test?
a: To find out which substance you are allergic to
So that you get better faster
So that the skin itches less
So that blood can be taken at the same time
112488.e: Drops with different allergens, such as pollen, animal hair or mites, are placed on the forearm. The spot where a weal appears shows the trigger.
112488.m: The skin prick test shows which substances you are allergic to.

112489.q: Why does the skin itch during an allergic reaction in a skin prick test?
a: The body releases the substance histamine
The light in the room irritates the skin
112489.e: In an allergy, immune cells release histamine. It makes the skin red, causes a weal and triggers itching.
112489.m: In allergies, histamine causes redness and itching.

112490.q: Which medicines must you stop taking for a few days before a skin prick test?
112490.e: Medicines against histamine suppress the skin reaction. The test could then wrongly come out negative.
112490.m: Before a skin test, stop allergy medicines after talking to the doctor.

112491.q: Why is a patch test for contact allergies such as nickel only read after two to three days?
a: Contact allergies only show up after a delay
The patch has to dry first
The doctor has no time before then
The nickel has to rust first
112491.e: With contact allergies, the skin does not react straight away but only after hours or days. That is why the test patches stay on the back for longer.
112491.m: Contact allergies only show up after some time.

112492.q: Which examination can add to or replace a skin test for allergies?
112492.e: Special antibodies against individual allergens can be measured in the blood. This is useful when a skin test is not possible, for example with a severe skin rash.
112492.m: Allergies can also be detected with a blood test.

112493.q: Which foods most often cause allergies in young children?
112493.e: Cow’s milk and hen’s eggs are among the most common allergy triggers in babies and young children. Rice and many vegetables, on the other hand, are rarely a problem.
112493.m: In young children, milk and egg are common allergy triggers.

112494.q: What is the body missing in lactose intolerance?
