113147.m: Muscles grow during the recovery time after training.

113148.q: What is the principle called that the body recovers beyond its old level after a load?
113148.e: After training, the body does not just recover; it becomes a little more capable than before. This is called supercompensation.
113148.m: Through supercompensation, the body becomes stronger after training.

113149.q: What happens to muscles that are not used for weeks, for example because of a plaster cast?
113149.e: Unused muscles become thinner and weaker; this is called muscle wasting (atrophy). With training they can be built up again.

113150.q: Why is enough sleep important for building muscle?
113150.e: During sleep, the body releases growth hormones and repairs the muscles that have been worked. Too little sleep slows down muscle building.
113150.m: During sleep, the body recovers and repairs itself.

113151.q: Roughly how many skeletal muscles does a human have?
113151.e: Depending on how they are counted, humans have more than 600 skeletal muscles; the figure of around 650 is often given.
113151.m: Humans have more than 600 skeletal muscles.

113152.q: Which type of muscle do you move at will and build up through strength training?
a: Smooth muscle of the blood vessels
113152.e: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones and can be controlled consciously. Heart muscle and smooth muscle work by themselves.
113152.m: Strength training builds up skeletal muscle.

113153.q: What is stretching called in which you hold a position calmly for several seconds?
113153.e: In static stretching, you hold the stretch without bouncing, for example for 20 to 30 seconds.
113153.m: In static stretching, you hold the position calmly.

113154.q: What is stretching with controlled swinging movements, such as leg swings, called?
113154.e: In dynamic stretching, you move deliberately into the stretch and out again. It is well suited to warming up.
113154.m: Dynamic stretching works with controlled movements.

113155.q: What should a correct stretch feel like?
a: A stabbing pain in the joint
113155.e: You only stretch until you feel a comfortable pull in the muscle. Pain is a warning signal that you have gone too far.
113155.m: Stretching should pull, but not hurt.

113156.q: Which muscle is stretched when you pull your heel towards your bottom while standing?
113156.e: Pulling the heel towards the bottom stretches the front of the thigh. That is where the four-headed thigh muscle, the quadriceps, is.
113156.m: Pulling the heel to the bottom stretches the front of the thigh.

113157.q: What should you do with your breathing when stretching?
a: Only force air out through the mouth
113157.e: Calm breathing helps the muscle relax. If you hold your breath, you tend to tense up.

113158.q: Which muscle is stretched when, in a lunge position, you keep your back heel on the floor and lean towards a wall?
113158.e: In this position, the back of the lower leg is stretched. That is where the calf muscle is.
113158.m: With your heel on the floor, you stretch the calf.

113159.q: Why should you not stretch with jerky bouncing?
a: It lowers the pulse too much
113159.e: Jerky bouncing triggers a protective reflex and can lead to small injuries in the muscle. It is better to stretch slowly and in a controlled way.

113160.q: Why do people stretch dynamically rather than holding long static stretches before a sprint?
a: Long holding can briefly reduce explosive strength
113160.e: Stretches held for a long time can make the muscles a little less explosive for a short while. That is why dynamic exercises are used before sprints and jumps.

113161.q: What is an injury from a blow or knock, which often causes a bruise, called?
113161.e: Contusions often happen in collisions, for example in football or ice hockey. Cooling and raising the injured part help against the swelling.
113161.m: A contusion is caused by a blow or knock.

113162.q: What is it called when a joint pops out of its normal position, for example in the shoulder?
113162.e: In a dislocation, the joint surfaces lose contact. The joint must be put back in place by a specialist.
113162.m: If a joint pops out of place, it is called a dislocation.

113163.q: Which ligament in the knee is particularly often torn in skiing and football injuries?
113163.e: The anterior cruciate ligament stabilises the knee during twisting movements. It often tears in falls with a twisted knee.
113163.m: The anterior cruciate ligament is a common injury in skiing and football.

113164.q: Which tendon connects the calf muscle to the heel bone?
113164.e: The Achilles tendon is the strongest tendon in the body. It transfers the force of the calf to the heel.
113164.m: The Achilles tendon connects the calf and the heel.

113165.q: What helps most to prevent sports injuries?
113165.e: After warming up, body and mind are ready for the effort. This lowers the risk of strains and tears.

113166.q: What is the common injury called when you go over on the outside edge of your foot?
a: A ligament injury in the ankle
113166.e: When you go over on your ankle, the outer ligaments of the ankle joint are overstretched or torn. This is one of the most common sports injuries.
113166.m: Going over on your ankle often injures the ankle ligaments.

113167.q: What is overstretching of muscle fibres without a tear called?
113167.e: In a strain, muscle fibres are overstretched but not torn. If fibres tear, it is called a torn muscle fibre.
113167.m: A strain is an overstretching of the muscle.

113168.q: What is a broken bone called that is caused by many small overloads rather than an accident?
113168.e: If you run too much without enough recovery, the bone can get fine cracks. These can turn into a stress fracture, often in the foot.
113168.m: Too much load without a break can cause a stress fracture.

113169.q: What does the abbreviation J+S stand for in Swiss sport?
113169.e: Jugend+Sport (Youth+Sport) is the Confederation’s largest sports promotion programme for children and young people in Switzerland.

113170.q: Which federal office is responsible for Jugend+Sport?
a: The Federal Office of Public Health
113170.e: Jugend+Sport is run by the Federal Office of Sport (FOSPO). It supports sports courses in clubs, schools and camps.
113170.m: The Federal Office of Sport runs Jugend+Sport.

113171.q: In which place in the canton of Bern is the Swiss Federal Institute of Sport?
113171.e: The institute is in Magglingen above Biel. The Federal Office of Sport also has its headquarters there.
113171.m: The Swiss Federal Institute of Sport is in Magglingen.

113172.q: Which age group is Jugend+Sport intended for?
113172.e: Jugend+Sport is aimed at children and young people aged 5 to 20. For the little ones, there is J+S children’s sport.
113172.m: Jugend+Sport is for children and young people aged 5 to 20.

113173.q: What is a person called who may lead sports courses after J+S training?
113173.e: Anyone who has attended a J+S leaders’ course becomes a J+S leader. After that, you must take further training regularly.
113173.m: J+S leaders run recognised sports courses.

113174.q: What is the aim of Jugend+Sport?
a: To get children and young people excited about sport
113174.e: Jugend+Sport supports sports courses and camps so that as many children and young people as possible enjoy doing sport regularly.
113174.m: Jugend+Sport wants to get children and young people excited about sport.

113175.q: Where in Ticino is the Confederation’s national youth sports centre?
113175.e: The Centro Sportivo Nazionale della Gioventù is in Tenero on Lake Maggiore. Many camps and courses take place there.
113175.m: The national youth sports centre is in Tenero.

113176.q: What do clubs receive from the Confederation when they run recognised J+S courses?
113176.e: The Confederation pays contributions for recognised J+S courses and camps. This allows clubs to offer cheap activities for children.
113176.m: For J+S courses, the Confederation pays clubs contributions.

113177.q: Why do endurance athletes often train in the mountains?
113177.e: At altitude the air pressure is lower, so you breathe in less oxygen with each breath. Over time, the body adapts to this lack.
113177.m: Altitude training uses the thin air in the mountains.

113178.q: Which blood cells does the body produce more of during altitude training?
113178.e: When oxygen is short, the body makes more of the cells that carry oxygen. This lets the blood bring more oxygen to the muscles.
113178.m: At altitude, the body makes more red blood cells.

113179.q: Which hormone stimulates the production of red blood cells and is banned as a doping substance when injected?
113179.e: Erythropoietin (EPO) is produced naturally in the kidney. Given artificially, it is banned in sport.
113179.m: EPO stimulates the production of red blood cells.

113180.q: Which place in the Grisons at over 1,800 metres is known for altitude training?
113180.e: St Moritz is in the Upper Engadine at over 1,800 metres above sea level. Many runners and cross-country skiers train there at altitude.
113180.m: St Moritz is a well-known place for altitude training.

113181.q: What do you often notice during sport in the first few days at high altitude?
a: You get out of breath more quickly
113181.e: Because less oxygen arrives with each breath, you get tired more quickly with the same effort. After a few days, the body gets used to it.
113181.m: At high altitude, you get out of breath more quickly at first.

113182.q: What does the principle “live high, train low” describe?
a: Sleep high up, train lower down
Sleep lower down, train high up
113182.e: You live at altitude so that your blood adapts, but train lower down, where you can train harder.
113182.m: With “live high, train low”, you sleep high up and train lower down.

113183.q: What are health problems such as headaches and nausea when climbing too quickly to high altitudes called?
113183.e: If you climb too quickly to high altitudes, the body cannot adapt. Headaches and nausea are typical signs of altitude sickness.
113183.m: Climbing too quickly can cause altitude sickness.

113184.q: How long does an altitude training camp usually need to last at least to have an effect?
113184.e: The body needs time to make more red blood cells. Altitude training camps therefore often last two to four weeks.
113184.m: Altitude training needs several weeks to work.

113185.q: What is the endurance called that forms the basis for almost all sports and is built up with easy training?
113185.e: Basic endurance allows long efforts at medium intensity. It also helps you recover faster between hard sessions.
113185.m: Basic endurance is the foundation for many sports.

113186.q: What is the ability to adjust quickly to a new situation, for example when the ball bounces off unexpectedly, called?
113186.e: Adaptability lets you change a movement in a flash. It is particularly important in ball games.

113187.q: Why are the wrists particularly at risk when inline skating?
a: Because you often catch yourself with your hands when you fall
Because you move your hands while skating
Because the wheels rub against your hands
Because your hands sweat while skating
113187.e: When you fall, you stretch out your hands by reflex. Wrist guards prevent fractures and grazes when this happens.
113187.m: When inline skating, wrist guards protect against injuries.

113188.q: Why should you warm up your body briefly before stretching?
a: So that your pulse goes down
113188.e: Warmed-up muscles have a better blood supply and are more elastic. They can be stretched more easily and with less risk of injury.
113188.m: Warm muscles stretch better than cold ones.

114063.q: What does the abbreviation REM in REM sleep stand for?
114063.e: REM stands for “Rapid Eye Movement”. In this sleep phase, the eyes move quickly back and forth under the closed eyelids.
114063.m: REM stands for the rapid eye movements during sleep.

114064.q: In which sleep phase do we dream particularly vividly and in pictures?
114064.e: People woken from REM sleep usually report vivid, story-like dreams. Dreams also occur in other phases, but they are usually fainter there.
114064.m: We have our most vivid dreams in REM sleep.

114065.q: What happens to most skeletal muscles during REM sleep?
114065.e: In REM sleep, the skeletal muscles are largely paralysed. This stops us actually carrying out the movements from our dreams.
114065.m: In REM sleep, the muscles are relaxed so that we do not act out our dreams.

114066.q: Why is REM sleep also called “paradoxical sleep”?
a: The brain is almost as active as when awake
You sleep with your eyes open
You do not breathe at all
114066.e: Although the body is deeply asleep, the brain in REM sleep shows a pattern of activity similar to being awake. This apparent contradiction gave the phase its name.
114066.m: In paradoxical sleep, the body is still but the brain is very active.

114067.q: Roughly what share of a night does REM sleep make up in adults?
114067.e: In healthy adults, REM sleep makes up around a fifth to a quarter of sleeping time. We spend most of the night in non-REM sleep.
114067.m: Adults spend about a fifth to a quarter of the night in REM sleep.

114068.q: Who spends a particularly large amount of sleeping time in REM sleep, about half?
114068.e: In newborn babies, active sleep, which corresponds to REM sleep, makes up about half of their sleep. This share decreases as they get older.
114068.m: Babies spend much more time in REM sleep than adults.

114069.q: When in the night do the REM phases last longest?
a: They are always the same length
114069.e: The first REM phase of the night is often only a few minutes long. The REM phases get longer from cycle to cycle, which is why we often remember dreams in the morning.
114069.m: The REM phases get longer and longer as the night goes on.

114070.q: Roughly how many REM phases do you have in a night?
114070.e: A sleep cycle lasts about 90 minutes and usually ends with a REM phase. In one night, you go through 4 to 6 such cycles.
114070.m: There are several REM phases each night.

114071.q: How do heartbeat and breathing typically behave during REM sleep?
114071.e: In REM sleep, pulse and breathing vary more than in calm deep sleep. This fits with the high activity of the brain in this phase.
114071.m: In REM sleep, heartbeat and breathing become more irregular.

114072.q: How do brain waves change in deep sleep?
114072.e: If you measure brain activity in deep sleep, large, slow waves appear. The brain is then particularly calm.
114072.m: In deep sleep, the brain oscillates slowly.

114073.q: In which part of the night is deep sleep most common?
a: In the first half of the night
In the second half of the night
114073.e: The longest deep sleep phases occur in the first sleep cycles. Towards morning there is hardly any deep sleep, but more REM sleep.
114073.m: We get most of our deep sleep in the first half of the night.

114074.q: Which hormone is released in larger amounts mainly during deep sleep?
114074.e: The pituitary gland releases a lot of growth hormone, especially in the first deep sleep phases. It is important for growth and the repair of tissue.
114074.m: In deep sleep, the body releases a lot of growth hormone.

114075.q: How do you usually feel when you are woken from deep sleep?
114075.e: It is hard to wake up from deep sleep, and you need a few minutes to think clearly. This state is called sleep inertia.
114075.m: People woken from deep sleep are often groggy.

114076.q: How do pulse and blood pressure typically change in deep sleep?
114076.e: In deep sleep, the body is at its most relaxed. Heartbeat, blood pressure and breathing become slow and even.
114076.m: In deep sleep, the heart and circulation calm down.

114077.q: Which task for learning is particularly linked to deep sleep?
114077.e: In deep sleep, things learned during the day, such as vocabulary and facts, are consolidated in the memory. That is why sleep helps after learning.
114077.m: In deep sleep, the brain consolidates what it has learned.

114078.q: How does the share of deep sleep change with increasing age?
a: It disappears by the age of 10
114078.e: Children and teenagers have a lot of deep sleep. In older people there is much less of it, and sleep becomes lighter and is interrupted more often.
114078.m: With age, there is less deep sleep.

114079.q: Which sleep phase is considered the most restorative for the body?
114079.e: In deep sleep, the body is at its most relaxed. It recovers, repairs tissue and releases growth hormone.

114080.q: Roughly how long does a complete sleep cycle last in adults?
114080.e: A cycle of light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep lasts around 90 minutes. Then the next cycle begins.
114080.m: A sleep cycle lasts about an hour and a half.

114081.q: Roughly how many sleep cycles do you go through in a normal night?
114081.e: With around 7 to 9 hours of sleep and about 90 minutes per cycle, that makes about 4 to 6 cycles. Each cycle is made up a little differently.
114081.m: In one night, the sleep cycles repeat four to six times.

114082.q: Into which two main types is sleep divided?
114082.e: A distinction is made between REM sleep with rapid eye movements and non-REM sleep. Non-REM sleep includes the falling-asleep phase, light sleep and deep sleep.
114082.m: Sleep consists of REM sleep and non-REM sleep.

114083.q: How long do healthy people usually take to fall asleep?
a: A few minutes to about half an hour
114083.e: The time from turning off the light to falling asleep is called sleep latency. In healthy people it is usually only a few minutes to about half an hour.
114083.m: Healthy people usually fall asleep within half an hour.

114084.q: Which sleep phase takes up the largest part of the night in adults?
114084.e: Light sleep makes up about half of all sleeping time. It occurs in every sleep cycle.
114084.m: We spend about half the night in light sleep.

114085.q: How can a sleep laboratory tell which sleep phase someone is in?
114085.e: Each sleep phase has typical patterns in the brain waves. In light sleep, for example, you see short bursts of waves called sleep spindles.
114085.m: The brain waves reveal the sleep phase.

114086.q: Roughly what does the curve of the sleep phases of one night look like?
a: Like a staircase that goes up and down several times
114086.e: During the night you switch several times between light sleep, deep sleep and dream sleep. The curve showing this is called a hypnogram and looks like a staircase.
114086.m: The sleep phases alternate several times during the night.

114087.q: What is the sudden jerk of the body just as you fall asleep called?
114087.e: A hypnic jerk is a harmless, short twitch of the muscles in the falling-asleep phase. It often feels as if you are falling.
114087.m: A jerk while falling asleep is usually harmless.

114088.q: In which sleep stage are you easiest to wake up?
a: In the first deep sleep phase
114088.e: The falling-asleep phase N1 is the transition from being awake to sleep. Even quiet noises can wake you up again then.
114088.m: You wake up most easily in the falling-asleep phase.

114089.q: Roughly how long does one cycle of the internal clock that controls sleeping and waking last?
114089.e: The internal clock runs on a rhythm of about 24 hours. Experts call it circadian, from the Latin “circa dies”, about a day.
114089.m: The internal clock ticks on a daily rhythm.

114090.q: Roughly how long does a sleep cycle of light sleep, deep sleep and dream sleep last?
114090.e: In one night you go through several sleep cycles of about 90 minutes each. Such rhythms, which are shorter than a day, repeat several times.
114090.m: A sleep cycle lasts about an hour and a half.

114091.q: Which rhythm only repeats once a year?
114091.e: Some rhythms last much longer than a day. Hibernation or bird migration repeat every year.

114092.q: Which hormone makes us tired in the evening?
114092.e: When it gets dark, the body produces more melatonin. It signals to the internal clock that it is time to sleep.

114093.q: Which bird are people compared to who like getting up early and get tired early?
114093.e: Early risers are called “larks” and night people “owls”. These types are called chronotypes and are partly inborn.
114093.m: Early risers are larks, night people are owls.

114094.q: How does the internal clock shift in many teenagers?
a: They get tired later in the evening
They get tired as early as the afternoon
They no longer need any sleep
They wake up at 4 in the morning
114094.e: In adolescence, the sleep-wake rhythm shifts later. Many teenagers only get tired late and find it hard to get up in the morning.
114094.m: Teenagers often only get tired late in the evening.

114095.q: What does science say about the biorhythm theory of fixed cycles of 23, 28 and 33 days from birth?
114095.e: This theory claims that body, feelings and mind follow fixed cycles from birth. Studies could not confirm this; it is considered a pseudoscience.
114095.m: Fixed biorhythm curves from birth are not scientifically proven.

114096.q: When during the day is a person’s body temperature at its lowest?
a: In the early hours of the morning
114096.e: Body temperature varies by just under one degree over the course of the day. It reaches its lowest point in the second half of the night, usually a few hours before waking.
114096.m: The body is coolest in the early hours of the morning.

114097.q: Where in the body is the main control of the internal clock?
114097.e: The master clock is a tiny area deep in the brain. It lies directly above the place where the optic nerves cross.
114097.m: The body’s master clock is in the brain.

114098.q: Through which sense organ does the internal clock find out whether it is day or night?
114098.e: Special cells in the retina report the brightness directly to the master clock in the brain through their own nerve pathway. That is why even some blind people still set their internal clock by light.
114098.m: The eyes tell the internal clock how bright it is.

114099.q: When does the body produce a particularly large amount of the sleep hormone melatonin?
a: At night, when it is dark
114099.e: Melatonin is mainly produced in the dark and makes us tired. Bright light, including from screens, slows down its production.
114099.m: In the dark, the body produces the sleep hormone melatonin.

114100.q: Which time cue sets the internal clock most strongly?
114100.e: Light is the body’s most important timekeeper. Every day it resets the internal clock to the change between day and night.

114101.q: How long does the internal clock’s day usually last in humans when there are no time cues?
114101.e: Without daylight and clocks, the internal clock in most people runs a little longer than 24 hours. That is why it has to be reset by light every day.
114101.m: The internal clock usually runs a bit slower than a 24-hour day.

a: A timekeeper in the body for the daily rhythm
A bone in the inner ear
An alarm clock in the bedroom
114102.e: The internal clock controls when we are tired or awake, when we are hungry and how warm our body is. It runs on a rhythm of about 24 hours.
114102.m: The internal clock controls our daily rhythm.

114103.q: What was found in people who lived for weeks without daylight or clocks in a bunker?
a: They kept sleeping and waking regularly
114103.e: In bunker experiments, people kept a sleep-wake rhythm of a little more than 24 hours. This proved that we have our own internal clock.
114103.m: Bunker experiments proved that humans have their own internal clock.

114104.q: Do plants have an internal clock too?
a: Yes, some open and close their leaves on a daily rhythm
No, only animals with a brain have one
114104.e: A mimosa kept in a dark cupboard still kept opening and closing its leaves on a daily rhythm. That is how it was discovered that plants also have an internal clock.
114104.m: Plants also have an internal clock.

114105.q: Which hormone rises sharply in the morning and helps us wake up?
114105.e: Cortisol reaches its peak shortly after waking up. It provides energy and gets the body going.
114105.m: In the morning, the hormone cortisol wakes us up.

114106.q: How many hours of sleep per night do experts recommend for teenagers aged 13 to 18?
114106.e: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 8 to 10 hours of sleep for teenagers. Many teenagers sleep much less on school days.
114106.m: Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep.

114107.q: What is the short, unintended nodding off called that is dangerous when driving, for example?
114107.e: In a microsleep, you fall asleep for a few seconds without noticing. At 100 km/h, a car travels more than 80 metres in three seconds.
114107.m: Microsleep at the wheel is life-threatening.

114108.q: How does lack of sleep typically affect appetite?
a: You are not hungry at all
114108.e: With lack of sleep, the hunger hormone ghrelin rises and the fullness hormone leptin falls. That is why people often eat more after short nights.
114108.m: People who sleep too little are often hungrier.

114109.q: What happens when a person does not sleep for several days?
a: Concentration and memory get much worse
114109.e: In 1964, a school pupil stayed awake for eleven days. Towards the end, he had great difficulty with concentration, memory and speech.
114109.m: Long sleep deprivation badly weakens concentration and memory.

114111.q: Which defence system of the body is weakened by constant lack of sleep?
114111.e: People who constantly sleep too little fall ill more easily. During sleep, the immune system works particularly hard.
114111.m: Enough sleep strengthens the body’s defences.

114112.q: What is the accumulated lack of sleep after several nights that are too short called?
114112.e: Missing hours of sleep add up to a sleep debt. It can only partly be made up by having a lie-in at the weekend.
114112.m: Missing sleep builds up as sleep debt.

114113.q: Which ability at school suffers most from too little sleep?
114113.e: After nights that are too short, it is hard to stay attentive and learn new things. Well-rested pupils learn more easily.
114113.m: When well rested, you can concentrate better.

114114.q: What problem do people with insomnia have?
a: They find it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep
They suddenly fall asleep during the day
114114.e: With insomnia, people lie awake for a long time or keep waking up during the night.
114114.m: Insomnia means having trouble falling asleep or staying asleep.

114115.q: What are the rules and habits that encourage good sleep called?
114115.e: Sleep hygiene includes, for example, regular sleeping times, a dark, quiet room and no caffeine in the evening.
114115.m: Good sleep hygiene helps you fall asleep.

114116.q: Why does coffee keep you awake?
a: Caffeine blocks a tiredness substance in the brain
Coffee contains a great deal of sugar
114116.e: While you are awake, the substance adenosine builds up in the brain and makes you tired. Caffeine blocks its docking sites and so keeps you awake.
114116.m: Caffeine blocks tiredness in the brain.

114117.q: What do experts advise if you have not fallen asleep after about 20 minutes in bed?
a: Get up and do something calm
Do sport until you are exhausted
114117.e: You should not link your bed with lying awake and brooding. So you get up briefly, do something calm and only go back to bed when you are tired.
114117.m: If you cannot fall asleep, it is better to get up for a while.

114118.q: What helps most with long-lasting insomnia?
a: A therapy that changes sleeping habits
Lots of coffee in the morning
114118.e: Experts first recommend a therapy that changes unhelpful habits and thoughts about sleep. It is called cognitive behavioural therapy.
114118.m: Better sleeping habits help against long-lasting insomnia.

a: When the sleep problems go on for months
When you go to bed late once
When you have a lie-in at the weekend
114119.e: Chronic means long-lasting. Insomnia is called chronic when the problems occur several times a week for at least three months.

114120.q: What risk do many sleeping pills have when taken for a long time?
114120.e: Some sleeping pills lose their effect over time and can lead to dependence. They should therefore only be taken for a short time and after talking to a doctor.
114120.m: Sleeping pills should only be taken briefly and on medical advice.

114121.q: What kind of thoughts keep many people with insomnia awake at night?
114121.e: Stress and thoughts going round in circles are among the most common causes of problems falling asleep. Relaxation exercises or writing down your worries can help.
114121.m: Brooding in bed makes it harder to fall asleep.

a: Travelling quickly across several time zones
Sitting on a train for too long
Eating too much on the plane
114122.e: If you fly quickly across several time zones, the time at your destination no longer matches your internal clock. The body then needs a few days to adjust.
114122.m: Jet lag happens when the internal clock and local time do not match.

114123.q: In which direction of flight is jet lag worse for most people?
114123.e: When flying east, the day becomes shorter and you have to sleep earlier. This is harder for the internal clock than a longer day when flying west.
114123.m: Flights east usually cause the worse jet lag.

114124.q: According to a rule of thumb, roughly how much can the internal clock adjust per day?
114124.e: As a rule of thumb, it is around one time zone per day. After a flight across six time zones, you need about six days to adjust completely.
114124.m: The internal clock only shifts by about one hour per day.

114125.q: What is the usual time difference between Zurich and New York?
114125.e: When it is 6 pm in Zurich, it is usually only 12 noon in New York. Only for a few weeks a year, when the clocks change on different dates, is the difference 5 hours.
114125.m: New York is usually six hours behind Zurich.

114126.q: What helps most after arrival to get over jet lag faster?
a: Getting plenty of daylight at your destination
Sleeping all day in the hotel
114126.e: Daylight is the internal clock’s most important time cue. If you spend time outdoors during the day at your destination, you adjust faster.
114126.m: Daylight at your destination helps against jet lag.

114127.q: Why is it already evening in Tokyo when it is midday in Zurich?
a: Tokyo is further east, where the sun rises earlier
All the clocks in Japan are wrong
Tokyo is in the southern hemisphere
Japan is closer to the sun
114127.e: The Earth turns from west to east. That is why the day starts earlier in the east, and Tokyo is several hours ahead of Switzerland.
114127.m: In the east, the day starts earlier.

114128.q: Why do you hardly get jet lag after a flight from Zurich to Johannesburg?
a: Both are almost in the same time zone
There is no clock time in Africa
114128.e: Johannesburg lies south of Zurich and has at most one hour’s time difference. The flight is long, but the internal clock hardly has to adjust.
114128.m: North-south flights cause hardly any jet lag.

114129.q: Which set of symptoms is typical of jet lag?
a: Tiredness during the day and lying awake at night
114129.e: With jet lag, you are tired or wide awake at the wrong time of day. Problems with concentration and digestion are often added.
114129.m: Jet lag makes you tired by day and awake at night.

114130.q: Which colour of light does the internal clock react to most strongly?
114130.e: In the eye there are sensory cells that react particularly to blue light. They tell the brain that it is daytime. Red light has hardly any effect on the internal clock.
114130.m: The internal clock reacts most strongly to blue light.

114131.q: What colour are the lenses of glasses that are meant to filter out blue light in the evening, usually?
114131.e: Yellow and orange lenses absorb a large part of the blue light. Blue or violet lenses, on the other hand, would let exactly this light through.
114131.m: Blue light filter glasses usually have yellowish or orange lenses.

114132.q: Which light sources give off a particularly large amount of blue light in the evening?
114132.e: The white LEDs in screens have a high proportion of blue. Candles and fire, on the other hand, glow yellowish-red with little blue.
114132.m: Phone screens give off a lot of blue light.

114133.q: What does the night mode on many phones do to the screen colour?
a: It makes it warmer and more yellowish
It makes it black and white
114133.e: Night mode reduces the proportion of blue and gives the picture a yellowish tint. But the most effective thing is to put the screen away completely before sleeping.
114133.m: Night mode makes the screen more yellowish.

114134.q: What does the kelvin figure on a light bulb packet show?
a: Whether the light looks warm or cold
How much electricity the bulb uses
114134.e: Warm white light has about 2,700 kelvin, cold daylight white over 5,000 kelvin. The higher the value, the more blue the light contains.
114134.m: The kelvin number shows the light colour of a bulb.

114135.q: Which lamp is better suited to the bedroom in the evening?
114135.e: Warm white light contains little blue and disturbs melatonin production less. This makes it easier to fall asleep.
114135.m: In the evening, warm, dimmed light is best.

114136.q: How long before sleeping do experts often recommend putting screens away?
114136.e: Light and exciting content keep the brain awake. That is why people are often advised not to use screens for about an hour before sleeping.
114136.m: An hour without screens before sleeping encourages good sleep.

114137.q: When is bright light rich in blue actually helpful for the internal clock?
a: In the middle of the night
114137.e: Bright light in the morning stops melatonin production and wakes you up. It sets the internal clock to an early start to the day.
114137.m: Bright light in the morning wakes you up.

114138.q: Roughly how long should a power nap last?
114138.e: A short sleep of 10 to 20 minutes refreshes you without falling into deep sleep. Afterwards you are quickly fit again.
114138.m: A power nap lasts no more than about 20 minutes.

114139.q: Why should a power nap not last much longer than 20 to 30 minutes?
a: Otherwise you go into deep sleep
114139.e: After about half an hour, deep sleep often begins. If you wake up from it, you feel worse instead of rested.
114139.m: A nap that is too long tends to make you more tired.

114140.q: At what time of day is a power nap best?
114140.e: After midday there is a natural dip in performance. A short sleep at this time disturbs night-time sleep the least.
114140.m: The after-lunch dip is a good time for a nap.

114141.q: What is the traditional midday rest in Spain called?
114141.e: The word siesta comes from the Latin “sexta hora”, the sixth hour after sunrise. It refers to midday.
114141.m: In Spain, the siesta is the midday rest.

114142.q: What helps to stop a power nap from getting too long?
114142.e: With an alarm set for about 20 minutes, you wake up before deep sleep begins. That way you feel fresh afterwards.
114142.m: An alarm keeps the power nap short.

114143.q: In which professional group did NASA study the effect of a short sleep of around 26 minutes in 1995?
114143.e: In the NASA study, pilots on long-haul flights slept briefly in the cockpit. Afterwards they were much more alert and reacted faster.
114143.m: A short sleep clearly increases alertness.

114144.q: What is a short sleep during the day called?
114144.e: A nap is a short, light sleep, often after lunch. The expression power nap emphasises its refreshing effect.
114144.m: A nap is a short sleep during the day.

114145.q: What helps to stop a short nap during the day from lasting too long?
114145.e: An alarm makes sure you wake up again after 10 to 20 minutes. That way the nap stays short and refreshing.
114145.m: An alarm keeps the nap short.

114146.q: What happens during an examination in a sleep laboratory?
a: Many body readings are measured at the same time during sleep
You learn to read faster on a course
114146.e: In the sleep laboratory, brain waves, eye movements, muscle tension, breathing and heartbeat are recorded, among other things. This makes it possible to detect sleep disorders.
114146.m: In the sleep laboratory, many readings are measured during sleep.

114147.q: How are brain waves measured in the sleep laboratory?
114147.e: Electrodes on the scalp measure the electrical activity of the brain. This measurement is called an EEG. It shows the sleep phases.
114147.m: Electrodes on the head measure brain waves.

114148.q: Why are eye movements also measured in the sleep laboratory?
a: Because they move quickly during dream sleep
To test how sharp your eyesight is
To find out your eye colour
Because otherwise the eyes dry out
114148.e: In REM sleep, when we dream a lot, the eyes move quickly back and forth. Electrodes next to the eyes record this.
114148.m: Rapid eye movements show dream sleep.

114149.q: What is measured in the sleep laboratory with electrodes on the chin and legs?
114149.e: Electrodes on the skin record the tension of the muscles. In REM sleep, muscle tension is very low.
114149.m: Electrodes on the chin and legs show how hard the muscles are working.

a: Breathing keeps stopping briefly during sleep
You grind your teeth at night
You suddenly fall asleep during the day
114150.e: In sleep apnoea, breathing keeps stopping briefly during sleep. People affected often snore loudly and are very tired during the day.
114150.m: In sleep apnoea, breathing stops during sleep.

114151.q: Which device is often used against sleep apnoea?
a: A breathing mask with slight positive pressure
114151.e: In CPAP therapy, a machine gently blows air into the airways through a mask. This keeps them open and the pauses in breathing disappear.
114151.m: A positive pressure mask keeps the airways open in sleep apnoea.

114152.q: What does a pulse oximeter on the finger measure during the night?
a: The oxygen saturation of the blood
114152.e: The pulse oximeter shines light through the finger and works out how much oxygen the blood is carrying. When breathing stops, this value falls.
114152.m: A pulse oximeter measures the oxygen in the blood.

114153.q: What happens in the illness narcolepsy?
a: You suddenly fall asleep during the day without wanting to
You cannot fall asleep at all at night
114153.e: People with narcolepsy have a disturbed control of sleeping and waking. They can fall asleep in the middle of everyday situations.
114153.m: With narcolepsy, sleep suddenly overwhelms you.

114154.q: Why did Switzerland introduce summer time?
a: To have the same time as its neighbouring countries
So that the cows would give more milk
114154.e: When the neighbouring countries had summer time and Switzerland did not, there were problems with train timetables and trade. That is why Switzerland has also had summer time since 1981.
114154.m: With summer time, Switzerland fell into line with its neighbours.

114155.q: What was Switzerland called in the summer of 1980 because it was the only country around without summer time?
114155.e: All the neighbouring countries had summer time in 1980, but Switzerland did not. This caused problems, for example with train timetables and trade.
114155.m: In 1980, Switzerland was a time island in Europe.

114156.q: On which day does summer time begin in Switzerland?
a: On the last Sunday in March
On the first Sunday in May
On the last Sunday in February
114156.e: On the last Sunday in March, the clock is put forward from 2 am to 3 am. Switzerland follows the EU rules on this.
114156.m: Summer time begins on the last Sunday in March.

114157.q: What happens to the length of your sleep on the night summer time begins?
a: The length of sleep stays the same
114157.e: The clock jumps from 2 am straight to 3 am. If you get up at the usual time, you have slept an hour less.
114157.m: In spring, the clock change costs you an hour of sleep.

114158.q: What is the standard time that applies in Switzerland in winter called?
114158.e: Central European Time (CET) is one hour ahead of universal time UTC. In summer, Central European Summer Time applies, two hours ahead.
114158.m: In winter, Central European Time applies in Switzerland.

114159.q: When was summer time first introduced in Europe?
114159.e: In 1916, in the middle of the First World War, Germany and Austria-Hungary introduced summer time. They wanted to save energy for lighting.
114159.m: Summer time has existed since the First World War.

114160.q: What was the original aim of summer time?
a: To make better use of daylight and save energy
To make the school holidays longer
114160.e: Putting the clock forward means it stays light for longer in the evening. This was supposed to mean less artificial light was needed. Today, however, the actual saving is disputed.
114160.m: Summer time was meant to help make better use of daylight.

114161.q: Which way do you turn the clock in spring when the clocks change?
114161.e: A well-known memory aid is “spring forward, fall back”. So in spring you put the clock forward, and in autumn you put it back.
114161.m: In spring you put the clock forward, in autumn back.

114450.q: Who is the first point of contact for most health problems?
a: The emergency department at the university hospital
114450.e: The family doctor looks after basic medical care. They treat many problems themselves and only refer patients on when necessary.
114450.m: For most problems, you go to the family doctor first.

114451.q: What is the letter called with which a family doctor sends a patient on to a specialist?
114451.e: With a referral, the family doctor sends a patient to a specialist. It says what needs to be investigated.
114451.m: A referral sends patients from the family doctor to a specialist.

114452.q: What is a big advantage of always going to the same family doctor?
a: She knows your whole medical history.
She is allowed to do every operation herself.
She does not need any examinations.
114452.e: If you go to the same family doctor for a long time, she knows you well. She knows about earlier illnesses, allergies and medicines.
114452.m: The family doctor knows her patients’ medical history best.

114453.q: What do you commit to with the family doctor model of Swiss health insurance?
a: Always going to your chosen family doctor first
114453.e: With the family doctor model, you always go to your chosen family doctor first, except in an emergency. In return, the premium is usually cheaper.
114453.m: With the family doctor model, you go to the family doctor first and pay a lower premium.

114454.q: Who is often the family doctor for children in Switzerland?
114454.e: Children and teenagers are often looked after by a paediatrician. She takes on the role of family doctor for them.
114454.m: For children, the paediatrician is often the family doctor.

114455.q: What is a visit by the doctor to a sick person at home called?
114455.e: On a home visit, the doctor comes to the patient’s home. This is important for people who can no longer get to the surgery.
114455.m: On a home visit, the doctor comes to the sick person’s home.

114456.q: What is a preventive check-up at the family doctor’s for?
114456.e: In a preventive check-up you are examined even if you feel healthy. This means illnesses can be found early and treated better.
114456.m: Preventive check-ups help to find illnesses early.

114457.q: Which instrument does the family doctor use to listen to the heart and lungs?
114457.e: With the stethoscope, the doctor listens to heart sounds and breathing sounds. This lets her detect pneumonia, for example.
114457.m: You listen to the heart and lungs with a stethoscope.

114458.q: Which specialist is responsible for heart diseases?
114458.e: The Greek word “kardia” means heart. Cardiologists examine and treat the heart and the circulation.
114458.m: Cardiology is the study of the heart.

114459.q: Which specialist do you go to with a bad skin rash?
114459.e: The Greek word “derma” means skin. Dermatologists treat skin diseases such as eczema or acne.
114459.m: The dermatologist is the skin doctor.

114460.q: What is an orthopaedic specialist responsible for?
114460.e: Orthopaedic specialists treat the musculoskeletal system. This includes bones, joints, ligaments and muscles.
114460.m: The orthopaedic specialist looks after the musculoskeletal system.

114461.q: What does the abbreviation ENT stand for in a specialist doctor’s title?
114461.e: An ENT doctor examines the ears, nose and throat. You go to her, for example, if you often have ear infections.
114461.m: The ENT doctor treats the ears, nose and throat.

114462.q: Which specialist treats diseases of the brain and nerves?
114462.e: The Greek word “neuron” means nerve. Neurologists treat epilepsy or migraine, for example.
114462.m: Neurology deals with the brain and nerves.

114463.q: Which specialist do you go to if you cannot see well?
114463.e: The eye doctor examines the eyes and prescribes glasses, for example. The technical term is ophthalmologist.
114463.m: For problems with sight, the eye doctor helps.

114464.q: Which specialist mainly treats children and teenagers?
114464.e: Paediatricians know all about children’s illnesses and development. The children’s doctor is called a paediatrician.
114464.m: The paediatrician is there for children and teenagers.

114465.q: What must a doctor in Switzerland do after studying medicine to become a specialist?
a: A one-year placement in a pharmacy
An exam set by the health insurer
114465.e: After their studies, young doctors work for several years in hospitals and practices. After this further training and an exam, they receive the title of specialist.
114465.m: After medical school, you become a specialist through several years of further training.

114466.q: Which specialist interprets X-rays and other images of the inside of the body?
114466.e: Radiologists are experts in imaging methods. They assess X-rays, CT and MRI scans.
114466.m: The radiologist assesses images of the inside of the body.

114467.q: What is the main task of surgery?
a: Treating diseases and injuries by operating
114467.e: Surgeons treat patients with procedures on the body. The word comes from Greek and means something like handwork.
114467.m: In surgery, healing is done by operating.

114468.q: What is the branch of surgery called that mainly deals with injuries after accidents?
114468.e: Trauma surgery (traumatology) treats broken bones and other accident injuries. In Switzerland, it is particularly in demand after skiing and cycling accidents.
114468.m: Trauma surgery treats injuries after accidents.

114469.q: Why do surgeons wear gloves, masks and sterile clothing in the operating theatre?
a: So that no germs get into the wound
So that they do not catch a cold
So that they can be recognised more easily
So that the equipment does not get dirty
114469.e: An open wound is a way in for bacteria. Sterile clothing and instruments prevent dangerous wound infections.
114469.m: In the operating theatre, everything must be sterile so that no germs get into the wound.

a: Cutting off a part of the body
114470.e: In an amputation, a badly injured finger or foot is removed, for example. Afterwards a prosthesis can help.
114470.m: In an amputation, a part of the body is cut off.

a: An operation through very small cuts
An operation that lasts several days
114471.e: In minimally invasive procedures, surgeons work through small openings with a camera and fine instruments. This is also called keyhole surgery.
114471.m: Keyhole surgery only needs small cuts.

114472.q: What do you get before a big operation so that you feel nothing and sleep?
114472.e: Under general anaesthetic you sleep deeply and feel no pain. An anaesthetist monitors your breathing and heartbeat while this happens.
114472.m: An anaesthetic makes sure you feel nothing during the operation.

114473.q: What is it called when an organ from a donor is put into the body of a sick person?
114473.e: In a transplant, a kidney or a heart is transplanted, for example. In Switzerland, the Swisstransplant foundation coordinates organ donation.
114473.m: In a transplant, a donor organ is put in.

114474.q: What must a patient give before a planned operation, after a discussion explaining it?
114474.e: The doctor explains the benefits and risks of the procedure. Only when the patient agrees may the operation go ahead, except in emergencies.
114474.m: Before an operation, the patient’s consent is needed.

114475.q: Which organ was successfully transferred from one person to another for the first time in 1967?
114475.e: In 1967, the surgeon Christiaan Barnard in South Africa transplanted a human heart for the first time. Today, heart transplants are also possible in Switzerland.
114475.m: The first heart transplant succeeded in 1967.

114476.q: What does a general anaesthetic do?
a: You sleep deeply and feel no pain.
You stay awake but cannot speak.
You are tired for a week.
114476.e: Under general anaesthetic, consciousness and the feeling of pain are switched off. This means even big operations can be carried out without pain.
114476.m: Under general anaesthetic, you sleep deeply and feel no pain.

114477.q: What is the anaesthetic called that only numbs a small area of the body?
114477.e: With a local anaesthetic, a numbing drug is injected in one place. You stay awake but feel no pain there, for example at the dentist.
114477.m: A local anaesthetic only numbs a small area.

114478.q: What does the Greek word “anaesthesia” roughly mean?
114478.e: The prefix “an” means without, and “aisthesis” means sensation. Anaesthesia switches off the feeling of pain.

114479.q: What does a pulse oximeter on the finger measure during an anaesthetic?
a: The oxygen content of the blood
114479.e: The pulse oximeter shines red light through the finger. From this it calculates the pulse and how much oxygen the blood is carrying.
114479.m: The pulse oximeter measures the oxygen in the blood.

114480.q: Who is responsible for the anaesthetic in hospital?
114480.e: The anaesthetist puts the patient under and monitors breathing and circulation throughout the operation.
114480.m: The anaesthetist is responsible for the anaesthetic.

114481.q: How were operations usually carried out before anaesthesia was invented?
a: With the patient awake and in great pain
With an injection into the leg
Not at all, operations were forbidden
114481.e: Before anaesthesia, patients had to endure operations while fully conscious. That is why surgeons worked as fast as possible. Anaesthetics only became common from the middle of the 19th century.
114481.m: Before anaesthesia, operations were very painful.

114482.q: What does the anaesthetist particularly ask about in the discussion before an anaesthetic?
114482.e: Allergies, existing illnesses and medicines affect the choice of anaesthetic. This lets the anaesthetist avoid risks.
114482.m: Before an anaesthetic, the anaesthetist checks allergies and illnesses.

114483.q: What is a tube in an anaesthetic?
114483.e: Under deep anaesthesia, you often no longer breathe enough by yourself. The tube is placed in the windpipe, and a machine takes over the breathing.
114483.m: Under anaesthetic, you are ventilated through the tube.

114484.q: Where are the rays produced in an X-ray machine?
a: In an X-ray tube, when fast electrons hit metal
In a magnet that spins quickly
In a loudspeaker with very high notes
In a light bulb with coloured glass
114484.e: In the X-ray tube, electrons are greatly accelerated. When they crash into a metal plate (anode), X-rays are produced.
114484.m: X-rays are produced when fast electrons crash into metal.

114485.q: Why do the lungs appear dark on an X-ray?
a: They contain a lot of air, which hardly stops the rays.
114485.e: Air hardly weakens X-rays at all. So a lot of radiation passes through the lungs to the detector, and this area turns dark.
114485.m: The lungs are dark on an X-ray because they contain a lot of air.

114486.q: What do you often wear during an X-ray to protect other parts of the body from the radiation?
114486.e: Lead stops X-rays very well. A lead apron protects parts of the body that are not meant to be X-rayed.
114486.m: A lead apron protects you during an X-ray.

114487.q: Where are X-rays also used outside medicine?
a: In baggage checks at the airport
114487.e: Baggage scanners at the airport X-ray suitcases. This shows what is inside without opening the case.
114487.m: At the airport, suitcases are X-rayed.

114488.q: What type of radiation are X-rays?
114488.e: Like light, X-rays are electromagnetic waves. But they have much more energy and can therefore pass through the body.

114489.q: Why are X-rays only taken when really necessary?
a: In high doses the radiation can damage cells.
The machine needs a lot of water.
You are not allowed to eat afterwards.
114489.e: X-rays are ionising and can damage the genetic material of cells. That is why the dose is kept as small as possible.
114489.m: Only X-ray when necessary, because the radiation can damage cells.

114490.q: Which injury is very often checked with an X-ray?
114490.e: An X-ray shows whether a bone is broken and how the pieces lie. Then a decision is made about a plaster cast or an operation.

114491.q: Which radiation does a computed tomography (CT) scanner use?
114491.e: In a CT scanner, an X-ray tube circles around the body. The computer works out images from many X-ray pictures.

114492.q: What kind of images does a CT scan produce?
a: Films of the heartbeat with sound
114492.e: A CT shows the body as if cut into thin slices. From these, the computer can also work out 3D views.
114492.m: A CT shows the body in cross-sectional images.

114493.q: What does the Greek word “tome” in tomography mean?
114493.e: Tomography means roughly “writing a picture of a slice”. “Tome” means cut, and “graphein” means to write.
114493.m: Tomography means making images of slices.

114494.q: Why must you lie completely still during a CT scan?
a: Otherwise the images will be blurred
Otherwise you fall into the ring
114494.e: The machine takes many pictures one after the other. If you move, the pictures do not fit together and become blurred.
114494.m: During a CT, you lie still so the images are sharp.

114495.q: Why is a contrast medium sometimes injected for a CT scan?
a: So that blood vessels and organs show up better
So that you fall asleep faster
So that the machine is quieter
114495.e: The contrast medium blocks X-rays more than the surrounding tissue does. This makes blood vessels and organs stand out more clearly.
114495.m: Contrast media make vessels and organs easier to see in the image.

114496.q: What is an advantage of CT compared with magnetic resonance imaging?
a: There is no radiation at all.
It is completely silent and takes an hour.
You do not need a computer.
114496.e: A CT scan often takes only a few minutes. That is why it is often used in emergencies, for example after a serious accident.
114496.m: A CT is quick, so it is very useful in emergencies.

114497.q: What is a disadvantage of CT compared with a single normal X-ray?
114497.e: In a CT scan, a great many X-ray pictures are taken. So you receive much more radiation than with a single picture.
114497.m: A CT gives more radiation than a simple X-ray.

114498.q: How does the patient lie during a CT scan?
a: On a couch that moves through a ring
Standing in front of a wall
114498.e: The couch slowly moves the body through the ring-shaped opening. Inside the ring, the X-ray tube rotates all the way round.
114498.m: In a CT, you move through a ring on a couch.

114499.q: What does an MRI scanner use to produce its images?
a: A strong magnetic field and radio waves
114499.e: MRI uses a very strong magnetic field and radio waves. The hydrogen nuclei in the body send out signals, from which images are calculated.
114499.m: MRI works with a magnetic field and radio waves.

114500.q: Why must you remove all metal objects before an MRI scan?
a: The strong magnetic field attracts metal.
Metal immediately gets as hot as a pan.
114500.e: The magnetic field is much stronger than a fridge magnet. Objects containing iron can fly across the room and injure people.
114500.m: In the MRI room, metal is dangerous because the magnet attracts it.

114501.q: What do patients often notice during an MRI scan?
114501.e: When the magnetic coils switch, loud knocking and humming noises are produced. That is why you are given headphones or earplugs.
114501.m: An MRI is loud, so you wear ear protection.

114502.q: What is MRI particularly good for?
a: Soft tissues such as the brain, ligaments and cartilage
114502.e: MRI shows soft tissues with very good contrast. That is why it is often used to examine knee injuries or the brain.
114502.m: MRI shows soft tissues particularly well.

114503.q: In which unit is the strength of an MRI scanner’s magnetic field given?
114503.e: The unit of magnetic flux density is called the tesla. Normal MRI scanners have 1.5 or 3 tesla, which is tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth’s magnetic field.
114503.m: The strength of the MRI magnet is measured in tesla.

114504.q: What is a big advantage of MRI compared with CT?
114504.e: MRI works without ionising radiation. That is why it is gentle even when examinations are repeated.
114504.m: MRI does not expose the body to X-rays.

114505.q: Which Swiss chemist from ETH Zurich received the Nobel Prize in 1991 for work on nuclear magnetic resonance, which is also important for MRI?
114505.e: Richard Ernst developed nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy decisively further. His methods also helped in the development of magnetic resonance imaging.
114505.m: Richard Ernst from ETH received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1991.

114506.q: What does an MRI scanner use to produce images of the inside of the body?
114506.e: MRI works with a very strong magnetic field and radio waves. Unlike X-rays, there is no harmful radiation.
114506.m: An MRI takes pictures with a strong magnetic field.

a: A tube with a camera and a light
A device for measuring blood pressure
114507.e: An endoscope is a thin, often flexible tube with a light source and a camera. It lets you look inside the body.
114507.m: With an endoscope, you look inside the body with a camera and light.

114508.q: What does the Greek word “endoscopy” roughly mean?
114508.e: “Endon” means inside, and “skopein” means to look at. So in an endoscopy, you look inside the body.

114509.q: What is an endoscopy of the stomach called?
114509.e: In a gastroscopy, the endoscope is pushed through the mouth into the gullet and stomach. This shows inflammation, for example.
114509.m: A gastroscopy is an endoscopy of the stomach.

114510.q: What does the doctor examine in an arthroscopy, for example after a sports accident?
a: The inside of a joint such as the knee
114510.e: In an arthroscopy, a thin camera is pushed into a joint, often the knee. This shows injured ligaments or cartilage.
114510.m: In an arthroscopy, you look inside the joint.

114511.q: What else can the doctor do during an endoscopy, besides looking?
114511.e: Fine forceps can be passed through a channel in the endoscope. A tissue sample (biopsy) is taken this way and examined in the laboratory.
114511.m: During an endoscopy, tissue samples can be taken.

114512.q: What carries the light round the bends in a flexible endoscope?
114512.e: In glass fibres, light is reflected back again and again at the wall (total internal reflection). This lets it travel even through bent tubes.
114512.m: Glass fibres carry light round bends.

114513.q: Which body system is examined in a bronchoscopy?
114513.e: The bronchi are the branches of the windpipe in the lungs. In a bronchoscopy, you look into the windpipe and bronchi.
114513.m: In a bronchoscopy, you look into the airways.

a: You swallow a capsule with a built-in camera.
A camera is stuck onto your skin.
You wear a camera on your head.
114514.e: The small camera capsule travels through the intestine and takes lots of photos on the way. This even makes it possible to examine the small intestine.
114514.m: In a capsule endoscopy, you swallow a mini camera.

114515.q: What do you need a doctor’s prescription for?
a: To set up a health insurance company
114515.e: The pharmacy only hands out many medicines on prescription. This ensures that a doctor has checked the treatment.
114515.m: Prescription-only medicines are only available with a prescription.

114516.q: Who is allowed to write a prescription for medicines?
114516.e: Doctors write prescriptions after examining the patient. The pharmacy then hands out the medicine.
114516.m: Prescriptions are written by the doctor.

114517.q: What is written on a prescription, among other things?
a: The name of the medicine and the dose
114517.e: The prescription states the medicine, the amount and how often to take it. It also has the patient’s name and the doctor’s stamp and signature.
114517.m: A prescription names the medicine and the dose.

114518.q: Which authority decides in Switzerland whether a medicine requires a prescription?
114518.e: Swissmedic is the Swiss Agency for Therapeutic Products in Bern. It authorises medicines and puts them into dispensing categories.

114519.q: Which medicines can you only get on a doctor’s prescription in Switzerland?
114519.e: Antibiotics are prescription-only. Taken wrongly, they can do harm and make bacteria resistant.
114519.m: Antibiotics are only available on prescription.

114520.q: What is a special feature of many doctors’ surgeries in German-speaking Switzerland?
a: Doctors may hand out medicines directly.
Prescriptions must be ordered from the Federal Council.
Medicines are only available in hospital.
114520.e: In many cantons of German-speaking Switzerland there is self-dispensing. This means you get medicines directly at the doctor’s surgery instead of at the pharmacy.
114520.m: With self-dispensing, the doctor’s surgery hands out medicines directly.

114521.q: Where do you normally take a prescription to get your medicine?
114521.e: At the pharmacy you get the prescribed medicine in exchange for the prescription. The pharmacist also explains how to take it.
114521.m: You take a prescription to the pharmacy.

a: A prescription that is valid for several collections
114522.e: People with chronic illnesses often need the same medicine for a long time. With a repeat prescription, they can collect it several times during a certain period.
114522.m: With a repeat prescription, you collect a medicine several times.

a: A copy with the same active ingredient
114523.e: A generic contains the same active ingredient in the same amount as the original medicine. It may be sold once the patent has expired.
114523.m: A generic is a copy of a medicine with the same active ingredient.

114524.q: When may a company sell a generic version of a medicine?
a: When the patent protection of the original has expired
As soon as the original is one year old
114524.e: The original medicine is protected by a patent. A patent lasts at most 20 years; after that, other companies may copy the active ingredient.
114524.m: Generics only exist after the patent has expired.

114525.q: Why are generics usually cheaper than original medicines?
a: There are no costs for expensive research and development.
They are only half as strong.
They are only sold in small packs.
114525.e: The maker of the original put a lot of money into research and studies. Generic companies do not have to, and so can sell more cheaply.
114525.m: Generics are cheaper because there are no research costs.

114526.q: In what may a generic and the original medicine differ?
a: In colour, shape and inactive ingredients
In the amount of active ingredient
114526.e: The active ingredient and its amount must be the same. Inactive ingredients such as colourings or fillers, as well as the name and appearance, may be different.
114526.m: Generics have the same active ingredient but may look different.

114527.q: What must a generic prove before it is authorised?
a: That it works in the body in the same way as the original
That it is bigger than the original
That it only works at night
114527.e: Studies show that the active ingredient gets into the blood just as quickly and strongly. This is called bioequivalence.
114527.m: A generic must work in the same way as the original.

114528.q: Why do health insurers often recommend a generic instead of the original?
a: It works the same but costs less
It is made only from plants
114528.e: A generic contains the same active ingredient as the original and works in the same way. Because it is cheaper, healthcare costs go down.
114528.m: Generics work the same and are cheaper.

114529.q: What may a pharmacist in Switzerland do in many cases if an original medicine is written on the prescription?
a: Hand out a cheaper generic instead
114529.e: Pharmacists may replace an original with a generic, unless the doctor has expressly ruled this out. This lowers healthcare costs.
114529.m: The pharmacy may often replace an original with a generic.

a: Instructions for use that come with a medicine
A letter from the doctor to the health insurer
114530.e: The package leaflet is inside the medicine packet. It contains everything important for using the medicine safely.
114530.m: The package leaflet explains how to use a medicine correctly.

114531.q: What do you find in the package leaflet of a medicine?
114531.e: The package leaflet says how much to take and when. In Switzerland it is officially called the patient information.
114531.m: The package leaflet tells you the correct dose of a medicine.

114532.q: What does the “side effects” section in the package leaflet describe?
a: Where you can buy the medicine
114532.e: As well as the desired effect, a medicine can also have unwanted effects. These side effects are listed in the package leaflet.
114532.m: Side effects are unwanted effects of a medicine.

114533.q: What does it mean when a side effect is described as “rare” in the package leaflet?
a: Only very few people get it
114533.e: “Rare” means that only a few out of many thousands of people treated are affected. So most people notice nothing of it.
114533.m: Rare side effects affect only very few people.

114534.q: What are “contraindications” in the package leaflet?
a: Situations in which you must not take the medicine
114534.e: Contraindications name cases in which the medicine could do harm, for example if you are allergic to the active ingredient.
114534.m: Contraindications say when you must not take a medicine.

114535.q: What do “interactions” in the package leaflet describe?
a: How often you should change the packet
How the weather affects the skin
114535.e: Some medicines strengthen or weaken each other. Food or alcohol can also change the effect.
114535.m: Interactions show how medicines affect each other.

114536.q: In which languages must the patient information be available in Switzerland?
114536.e: The patient information must be available in the three main national languages. This means people in all parts of the country can read it.
114536.m: The patient information is available in German, French and Italian.

114537.q: What should you do if you do not understand something in the package leaflet?
a: Ask at the pharmacy or the doctor’s
114537.e: Pharmacists and doctors answer questions about medicines. This helps to avoid mistakes when taking them.
114537.m: If anything is unclear, ask at the pharmacy or the doctor’s.

114539.q: Which aid do Rega crews use on helicopter flights at night?
114539.e: Night vision goggles amplify the little light there is. This lets the crews spot obstacles such as cables even in the dark.
114539.m: At night, Rega crews fly with night vision goggles.

114540.q: What can Rega waive for its patrons?
a: The costs of rescue missions that no insurance pays
114540.e: If no insurance covers a Rega mission, Rega can waive the costs for patrons. This is a thank-you for their support.
114540.m: Patrons often do not have to pay for uncovered Rega missions themselves.

a: Through taxes from all the cantons
114541.e: Rega is a non-profit foundation. Millions of patrons pay a contribution every year and so make its work possible.
114541.m: Patron contributions are Rega’s most important source of money.

114542.q: What does Rega use to bring patients back from far-away countries?
114542.e: For long distances, Rega uses its own air ambulance jets. They have an intensive care unit on board.
114542.m: With air ambulance jets, Rega flies sick people home from abroad.

114543.q: What is a typical task of Rega helicopters?
a: Flying injured people quickly to hospital
114543.e: Rega helicopters fly emergency doctors to accident scenes and injured people to hospitals. In the mountains especially, this is often the fastest way.
114543.m: Rega helicopters take injured people quickly to hospital.

114544.q: Where is Rega’s headquarters with the Rega Centre?
114544.e: The Rega Centre is at Zurich Airport. The operations centre, the air ambulance jets and the administration are housed there.
114544.m: Rega has its headquarters at Zurich Airport.

114545.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for a road ambulance?
114545.e: 144 is the emergency number for ambulances. 117 is the police and 118 the fire brigade.
114545.m: For an ambulance in Switzerland, dial 144.

114546.q: Which specialist do you go to with asthma?
114546.e: Asthma is a disease of the airways. Lung specialists, also called pulmonologists, treat the lungs and bronchial tubes.
114546.m: With asthma, the lung specialist helps.

114547.q: Why did far fewer people die after operations from about 1870 onwards?
a: Wounds and instruments were made germ-free
Operations were only done at night
114547.e: Surgeons such as Joseph Lister began to clean wounds and instruments with germ-killing substances. This meant there were far fewer wound infections.
114547.m: Working germ-free made operations much safer.

114548.q: Why does the dentist sometimes take an X-ray of your teeth?
a: To find tooth decay between the teeth
To find out the colour of the teeth
114548.e: Decay between the teeth often cannot be seen from the outside. A small X-ray shows the holes early.
114548.m: Dentists also find tooth decay with X-rays.

114549.q: What is the examination called in which a camera is used to look inside the bowel?
114549.e: In a colonoscopy, an endoscope is pushed into the large intestine. Small growths can also be removed during it.
114549.m: A colonoscopy lets doctors look inside the bowel.

114834.q: Who is known as the “father of medicine”?
114834.e: The Greek doctor Hippocrates is seen as the founder of scientific medicine. He explained illnesses by natural causes instead of the anger of the gods.
114834.m: Hippocrates is called the father of medicine.

114835.q: What is the promise called that is named after Hippocrates and describes a doctor's duties?
114835.e: In the oath, a doctor promises among other things to help the sick and not to harm them. It is still a model for medical ethics today.
114835.m: The Hippocratic Oath describes the duties of doctors.

114836.q: How did medicine explain illnesses for a long time after Hippocrates?
a: As an imbalance of the body's fluids
114836.e: According to the theory of the four humours, we are made of blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. If their balance is upset, you become ill. This theory was accepted until the 19th century.
114836.m: The old theory of the four humours explained illness as an imbalance of body fluids.

114837.q: Which diet and way of life did Hippocratic medicine often recommend as the first treatment?
a: Eating in moderation, rest and exercise
Lots of meat and little sleep
Only water and no food at all
114837.e: Hippocratic doctors relied first on diet, meaning a healthy way of life with suitable food, rest and exercise. Only after that did they turn to medicines or operations.
114837.m: Hippocratic medicine relied on a healthy way of life.

114838.q: What was especially important to Hippocrates when treating patients?
114838.e: Hippocrates observed the sick carefully and wrote down how the illness developed. That was an important step towards scientific medicine.
114838.m: Hippocrates relied on careful observation of the sick.

114839.q: Where did the doctor Hippocrates come from?
114839.e: Hippocrates lived on the Greek island of Kos. He and his students wrote many medical books.
114839.m: Hippocrates was a doctor from ancient Greece.

114840.q: Roughly in which century did Hippocrates live?
114840.e: Hippocrates was born around 460 BC and died around 370 BC. So he lived during the Classical period of Greece.
114840.m: Hippocrates lived in the 5th century BC.

114841.q: In which present-day Swiss canton was the doctor Paracelsus born?
114841.e: Paracelsus was born around 1493 in Egg near Einsiedeln. Einsiedeln is in the canton of Schwyz.
114841.m: Paracelsus was born near Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz.

114842.q: Which famous saying about poisons goes back to Paracelsus?
114842.e: Paracelsus realised that almost any substance is harmful in too large an amount and can be harmless or even healing in a small amount. The amount is what matters.
114842.m: According to Paracelsus, the dose makes the poison.

114844.q: In which Swiss city was Paracelsus the city doctor in 1527 and taught at the university?
114844.e: Paracelsus became city doctor in Basel in 1527 and gave lectures at the university. After quarrels with colleagues he had to leave the city as early as 1528.
114844.m: Paracelsus was city doctor in Basel around 1527.

114845.q: What was unusual about Paracelsus's lectures in Basel?
a: He spoke German instead of Latin
He only read from the Bible
114845.e: Scholars taught in Latin at that time. Paracelsus gave his lectures in German so that more people could understand him.
114845.m: Paracelsus taught in German instead of Latin.

114846.q: Which science did Paracelsus combine with medicine by making remedies from minerals and metals?
114846.e: Paracelsus used chemical methods to make medicines from minerals and metals. That is why he is seen as a pioneer of modern pharmacology.

114847.q: In which century did Paracelsus work?
114847.e: Paracelsus lived from about 1493 to 1541. So his work falls in the first half of the 16th century, at the time of the Reformation.

114848.q: Which country did the doctor Edward Jenner come from?
114848.e: Edward Jenner was an English country doctor from Berkeley in the county of Gloucestershire. That is where he carried out his famous experiments.
114848.m: Edward Jenner was an English country doctor.

114849.q: Against which disease did Edward Jenner develop the first vaccination?
114849.e: Jenner passed on material from a related, harmless germ and so protected people against the dangerous disease. His method spread quickly throughout Europe.
114849.m: Jenner developed the first vaccination against smallpox.

114850.q: In which century did Edward Jenner carry out the first smallpox vaccination?
114850.e: Jenner vaccinated against smallpox for the first time in 1796, so at the end of the 18th century. His method spread quickly in Europe.
114850.m: The first smallpox vaccination took place at the end of the 18th century.

114851.q: Which harmless germ did Edward Jenner use to vaccinate against dangerous smallpox?
114851.e: Cowpox is mild in humans but protects against real smallpox. Jenner took the material from a blister of an infected woman.

114852.q: Which disease is now considered wiped out worldwide thanks to vaccinations?
114852.e: After worldwide vaccination campaigns, the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980. It all began with Jenner's vaccination.
114852.m: Smallpox was wiped out thanks to vaccinations.

114853.q: Where does the word “vaccination” come from?
a: From the Latin word for cow
From the Greek word for needle
From the Latin word for blood
From the English word for protection
114853.e: The Latin word “vacca” means cow. The name is a reminder of where the first vaccine came from.
114853.m: The word vaccination comes from the Latin word for cow.

114854.q: What did Edward Jenner notice about milkmaids in the countryside?
a: They did not get smallpox after having cowpox
They were never bitten by mosquitoes
114854.e: People knew that milkmaids were protected against smallpox after the harmless cowpox. Jenner tested this observation scientifically.
114854.m: Jenner's idea began with an observation of milkmaids.

114855.q: What is Jenner often called because of his groundbreaking work?
114855.e: Jenner's smallpox vaccination was the first scientifically tested vaccination. It laid the foundation for all later vaccines.
114855.m: Edward Jenner is known as the father of vaccination.

114856.q: Which country did Louis Pasteur come from?
114856.e: Louis Pasteur was born in 1822 in Dole in eastern France. He was a chemist and microbiologist.
114856.m: Louis Pasteur was a French scientist.

114857.q: What is the process called in which milk is heated briefly to kill germs?
114857.e: In pasteurisation, milk is heated briefly to about 72 to 75 degrees. Most germs die, but the taste stays almost the same.
114857.m: Pasteurisation is named after Louis Pasteur.

114858.q: Against which disease did Louis Pasteur successfully use a vaccine on a human for the first time in 1885?
114858.e: In 1885 Pasteur treated a boy who had been bitten by a rabid dog. The boy survived thanks to the vaccination.
114858.m: In 1885 Pasteur vaccinated a human against rabies for the first time.

114859.q: What was the name of the boy Louis Pasteur treated for rabies in 1885?
114859.e: Joseph Meister was nine years old and came from Alsace. He later worked as a caretaker at the Pasteur Institute.
114859.m: The first boy treated for rabies was called Joseph Meister.

114860.q: Which old idea did Louis Pasteur disprove using glass flasks with a long, curved neck?
a: That life arises by itself from dead matter
That light is made of particles
114860.e: In his swan-neck flasks, a boiled nutrient liquid stayed free of germs because dust and germs got stuck in the curved neck. So life only comes from life.
114860.m: Pasteur showed that life does not arise by itself from dead matter.

114861.q: What is the famous research institute called that Louis Pasteur founded in Paris in 1887?
114861.e: The Pasteur Institute was founded in 1887 and opened in 1888. It still researches infectious diseases and vaccines today.
114861.m: The Pasteur Institute in Paris goes back to Louis Pasteur.

114862.q: Which living things did Louis Pasteur identify as the cause of fermentation, for example in wine and beer?
114862.e: Pasteur showed that living microorganisms such as yeast cause fermentation. Before that, fermentation was thought to be a purely chemical process.
114862.m: Pasteur realised that microorganisms cause fermentation.

114863.q: Against which animal disease did Pasteur develop a vaccine for sheep and cattle in 1881?
114863.e: In 1881 Pasteur proved in a public experiment that vaccinated sheep survived anthrax. Unvaccinated animals died.
114863.m: Pasteur developed a vaccine against anthrax in 1881.

114864.q: Which present from his wife allowed the young country doctor Robert Koch to start his research?
114864.e: Koch's wife Emmy gave him a microscope. With it he examined blood samples and bacteria in his practice.
